claim: The United States bought Greenland from Denmark in 1946.
record: In 1946 the Truman administration secretly offered Denmark $100 million in gold for Greenland. Denmark declined, and the offer stayed out of public view for decades.

sources.title: Proposals for the United States to purchase Greenland
America has actually tried to acquire Greenland 3 other times, as early as 1867
sources.quote: President Harry Truman's administration formally offered Denmark $100 million in gold to buy Greenland

claim: In 1932 Australian soldiers armed with machine guns were sent to cull emus in Western Australia.
record: Farmers asked for help as emus ravaged wheat crops, and the army sent a small detachment with Lewis guns. The birds scattered, the kill count disappointed, and the operation was withdrawn.

sources.title: Looking back: Australia's Emu Wars
sources.quote: Early on the morning of 2 November 1932, the Seventh Heavy Battery of the Royal Australian Artillery alighted at Campion, WA, on to a hot red-dirt landscape about halfway between Perth and Kalgoorlie. There they unpacked two Lewis automatic machine guns and 10,000 rounds of ammunition.

claim: Viking warriors wore horned helmets into battle.
record: No horned helmet has ever been found from the Viking Age. The only near-complete Viking helmet, from Gjermundbu in Norway, is a plain rounded cap.
origin: The look was popularised by 19th-century Romantic art and Carl Emil Doepler's 1876 costumes for Wagner's Ring cycle.

claim: In 1919 a wave of molasses swept through Boston's North End, killing 21 people.
record: A storage tank holding over two million gallons burst on 15 January 1919. The wave reached an estimated 35 mph, flattened buildings and killed 21 people.

sources.title: The Great Molasses Flood of 1919: Date, Deaths & Facts
sources.quote: A fifteen-foot wall of syrup cascaded over Commercial Street at 35 miles per hour, obliterating all the buildings, people, horses and wagons in its path.

claim: Britain and France went to war in 1898 over a ruined fort on the White Nile.
record: A French column and a British-led flotilla met at Fashoda in September 1898, and both capitals talked of war. France backed down that November, and a 1899 agreement drew the line instead.

claim: Eastman Kodak kept its internal books on a 13-month calendar until 1989.
record: George Eastman adopted the International Fixed Calendar at Kodak in the 1920s: thirteen months of 28 days each, plus a spare 'Year Day'. The company kept using it for internal accounting until 1989.

sources.title: The Calendar
sources.quote: The Eastman Kodak company adopted the 13-month calendar in 1924 and they continued to use it until 1989.

claim: Convicted witches in Salem, Massachusetts, were burned at the stake in 1692.
record: Nineteen people convicted at Salem were hanged, and one man was pressed to death with stones. Burning was the European punishment for witchcraft, not the colonial one.
origin: Burnings in continental Europe and later fiction merged in popular memory with Salem.

claim: In 897 a pope put the exhumed corpse of one of his predecessors on trial.
record: Pope Stephen VI had the body of Pope Formosus dug up, dressed in vestments and propped on a throne for the Cadaver Synod. The corpse was found guilty.

sources.title: The Strange Case of Pope Formosus
sources.quote: In early 897, a bizarre event known as the “cadaver synod” occurred in St. John Lateran’s in Rome. The disinterred corpse of Pope Formosus (891–894) was brought before the then-reigning pontiff, Stephen VI (896–897), to be tried on a variety of charges.

claim: Benjamin Franklin proposed the wild turkey as the national bird of the United States.
record: Franklin never made a public proposal. In a private 1784 letter to his daughter he grumbled about the bald eagle's "bad moral character" and called the turkey "a much more respectable bird".

sources.title: Did Benjamin Franklin Want the National Bird To Be A Turkey?
sources.quote: although Benjamin Franklin defended the honor of the turkey against the bald eagle, he did not propose it become one of America's most important symbols.

origin: A private letter, widely quoted after his death, hardened into the story of a formal proposal.

claim: Roman emperor Vespasian taxed the urine collected from Rome's public urinals.
record: Tanners and launderers bought urine from Rome's public latrines for its ammonia, and Vespasian made the trade pay tax. When his son Titus grumbled, the emperor held a coin from the first payment under Titus's nose and asked if it smelled. The phrase pecunia non olet, 'money doesn't stink,' still carries the joke.

sources.title: Pecunia non olet
sources.quote: Vespasian imposed a urine tax on the distribution of urine from Rome's public urinals (the Roman lower classes urinated into pots, which were later emptied into cesspools).

sources.title: Suetonius, The Life of Vespasian (Loeb translation), ch. 23
sources.quote: When Titus found fault with him for contriving a tax upon public conveniences, he held a piece of money from the first payment to his son's nose, asking whether its odour was offensive to him.

claim: In 193 CE, Rome's Praetorian Guard auctioned off the imperial throne to the highest bidder.
record: With the throne vacant in March 193, the guard took bids at its camp. Didius Julianus, barred from entering, shouted offers from outside the gates and won with 25,000 sesterces per soldier. The senator-historian Cassius Dio called it a most disgraceful business; Julianus reigned just 66 days.

sources.title: Didius Julianus
sources.quote: After the murder of Pertinax on 28 March 193, the Praetorian guard announced that the throne was to be sold to the man who would pay the highest price.

sources.title: Cassius Dio, Roman History, Book 74 (Loeb translation)
sources.quote: For, just as if it had been in some market or auction-room, both the City and its entire empire were auctioned off.

claim: Royal tomb builders in ancient Egypt went on strike under Ramesses III because their grain rations were late.
record: In Ramesses III's 29th year, the Deir el-Medina crews who carved royal tombs downed tools and staged sit-ins at temples, shouting 'We are hungry!' The scribe Amennakht logged the protest on a papyrus now in Turin's Museo Egizio, often called the earliest recorded strike.

sources.title: Strike Papyrus (Cat. 1880)
sources.quote: It is a report concerning a strike held during the reign of King Ramesses III in the village of Deir el-Medina. The workers protested because they had not received their regular food rations, which constituted payment for their work in the Valley of the kings.

sources.title: Deir el-Medina strikes
sources.quote: The Deir el-Medina strikes were a series of strikes by the artisans who worked on the tombs in the Egyptian Valley of the Kings, the most notable of which occurred in the 29th year of the reign of Ramesses III (circa 1158 BC).

claim: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Apollo 11 Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
record: Khufu's pyramid rose around 2600 BCE, roughly 2,500 years before Cleopatra was born in 70 or 69 BCE. Apollo 11 touched down in 1969, about 2,040 years after her birth. To Egypt's last Ptolemaic queen, Giza was already a relic of deep antiquity.

sources.title: Did Cleopatra Really Live Closer In Time To The First Lunar Landing Than The Great Pyramids?
sources.quote: Cleopatra was born ~2,500 years after the Great Pyramid at Giza was built, and ~2,000 years before the first lunar landing.

sources.title: Great Pyramid of Giza
sources.quote: It was built c. 2600 BC over a period of about 26 years.

sources.title: Cleopatra - Life, Rule & Death
sources.quote: Born in 70 or 69 B.C., Cleopatra was a daughter of Ptolemy XII (Auletes), a descendant of Ptolemy I Soter, one of Alexander The Great’s generals and the founder of the Macedonian Dynasty in Egypt.

claim: Hero of Alexandria designed a coin-operated machine that dispensed holy water in the 1st century CE.
record: A coin dropped through a slot landed on a small pan, tipping a lever that opened a valve and let the liquid flow. When the coin slid off, a counterweight snapped the valve shut. Hero described the device for temples, where worshippers washed before entering.

sources.title: Vending machine
sources.quote: The earliest known reference to a vending machine is in the work of Hero of Alexandria, an engineer and mathematician in 1st century AD Roman Egypt. His machine accepted a coin and then dispensed wine or holy water.

sources.title: Coin-Operated Holy Water Dispensing Machine
sources.publisher: Smith College Museum of Ancient Inventions
sources.quote: Designed by the Greek inventor Heron, this coin-operated holy water dispenser was used in Egyptian temples to dispense water for ritual washings.

claim: In 132 CE, China's Zhang Heng built an earthquake detector with dragons that dropped balls into toads' mouths.
record: Eight dragon heads ringed a bronze vessel; a tremor made one release its ball into the toad below, showing the quake's direction. The Book of Later Han says it once triggered with no shaking felt in the capital, and days later a messenger arrived reporting an earthquake in Longxi.

sources.title: Zhang Heng
sources.quote: To indicate the direction of a distant earthquake, Zhang's device dropped a bronze ball from one of eight tubed projections shaped as dragon heads; the ball fell into the mouth of a corresponding metal object shaped as a toad, each representing a direction like the points on a compass rose.

sources.title: The ancient earthquake detector that puzzled modern historians
sources.quote: Mounted on the outside of this were eight dragons, each with a bronze ball clasped within its jaw. Directly underneath these mythical protrusions were eight bronze toads, mouths agape to receive the balls if they fell.

claim: Roman emperor Nero cut a shipping canal through Greece's Isthmus of Corinth in 67 CE.
record: Nero broke the ground with a pickaxe and carried off the first basket of soil, and 6,000 Judean prisoners began cutting trenches from both ends. The dig was abandoned in 68, the year Nero died, and ships had to wait until 1893.

sources.title: Corinth Canal
sources.quote: The emperor Nero was the first to attempt to construct the canal, personally breaking the ground with a pickaxe and removing the first basket-load of soil in 67 AD, but the project was abandoned when he died shortly afterwards.

sources.title: Suetonius, The Life of Nero (Loeb translation), ch. 19
sources.quote: at a signal given on a trumpet he was first to break ground with a mattock and to carry off a basketful of earth upon his shoulders.

sources.title: The Wars of the Jews, Book III (Whiston translation)
sources.quote: Out of the young men he chose six thousand of the strongest, and sent them to Nero, to dig through the Isthmus, and sold the remainder for slaves

claim: Julius Caesar invaded the Parthian Empire with 16 legions in 44 BCE.
record: Sixteen legions and 10,000 cavalry were mobilized, six legions were already training in Macedonia, and Caesar was due to leave Rome on 18 March 44 BCE. He was assassinated on the Ides of March, three days before departure, and the eastern campaign never began.

sources.title: Julius Caesar's planned invasion of the Parthian Empire
sources.quote: Caesar intended to leave Rome to start the campaign on 18 March; however, three days prior to his departure he was assassinated.

sources.title: Appian, The Civil Wars, Book 2 (Loeb translation)
sources.quote: He sent across the Adriatic in advance sixteen legions of foot and 10,000 horse.

claim: In 97 CE, a Han Chinese envoy named Gan Ying reached the Roman Empire.
record: General Ban Chao sent Gan Ying west to Da Qin, the Chinese name for Rome. He reached a great sea on Parthia's edge, most likely the Persian Gulf, but Parthian sailors warned the crossing could take two years and drive men to homesickness and death. He turned back.

sources.title: Gan Ying
sources.quote: When [Gan] Ying heard this, he discontinued (his trip).

sources.title: The Western Regions according to the Hou Hanshu (trans. John E. Hill)
sources.publisher: Silk Road Seattle, University of Washington
sources.quote: These included the reports of his father's envoy, Gan Ying, who reached the shores of the Persian Gulf in 97 CE, and gathered what information he could on the Roman Empire.

claim: Athens conquered the Sicilian city of Syracuse in 414 BCE during the Peloponnesian War.
record: Athenian siege walls had all but encircled Syracuse, and its citizens were about to hold an assembly on ending the war when a lone Corinthian ship arrived with news that Spartan help was coming. The Spartan Gylippus rallied the defense, and by 413 BCE the Athenian expedition had collapsed.

sources.title: Sicilian Expedition
sources.quote: After Nicias defeated the attack, the Athenians finally extended their wall to the sea, completely blockading Syracuse by land, and their fleet entered the harbour to blockade them from sea.

sources.title: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 7 (trans. Richard Crawley)
sources.quote: Gongylus found the Syracusans on the point of holding an assembly to consider whether they should put an end to the war.

claim: In 227 BCE, the assassin Jing Ke killed King Zheng of Qin with a dagger hidden inside a rolled-up map.
record: As the king unrolled the map, Jing Ke seized the dagger and grabbed his sleeve, but the sleeve tore away. The king fled around a pillar until he could draw his long ceremonial sword and cut the assassin down. He went on to unify China as Qin Shi Huang.

sources.title: Jing Ke
sources.quote: When the King Zheng unrolled the map, Jing Ke immediately seized the revealed dagger, grabbed the king's sleeve and attacked him, who somehow managed to back away from the initial thrust by tearing off the sleeve in the process.

sources.title: Assassination as a Symptom
sources.quote: His mission failed, and his death only hastened the unification of China under Qin rule.

sources.title: Commemorating a Failed Assassin: The Making of the Jing Ke Lore in Early China
sources.quote: Once in the Qin court, Jing Ke drew the dagger and attempted to capture the king alive. He failed and was instead executed.

claim: Assyrian king Sennacherib captured Jerusalem during his invasion of Judah in 701 BCE.
record: Sennacherib's army besieged 46 fortified towns of Judah, and his own prism boasts that he shut King Hezekiah inside Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage.' But the city never fell: Hezekiah paid a huge tribute and gave up neighboring lands, and the Assyrians went home.

sources.title: Sennacherib's campaign in the Levant
sources.quote: Having captured most of Judah's settlements, the Assyrians trapped Hezekiah in Jerusalem, but did not take the city itself—Hezekiah was allowed to remain in power as King of Judah in exchange for paying a large tribute to the Assyrians and also surrendering adjacent lands, which were then redistributed to Assyrian vassals in Ekron, Gaza, and Ashdod.

sources.title: Hezekiah's Defeat: The Annals of Sennacherib on the Taylor, Jerusalem, and Oriental Institute Prisms
sources.quote: After destroying Ashkelon, further down the Mediterranean coast, the Assyrian army marched into Judah, laid siege to Lakhish and Jerusalem, and eventually cowed Judah into giving a large tribute from the treasuries of the king and Temple.

sources.title: Assyrian siege of Jerusalem
sources.quote: Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem, but did not capture it.

claim: Alexander the Great led his army east across northern India to the Ganges River in 326 BCE.
record: At the Hyphasis (Beas) River in Punjab, Alexander's exhausted soldiers refused to march on toward the Ganges. He withdrew to his tent for three days, then declared the omens unfavorable, had twelve great altars built to the Olympian gods, and turned back.

sources.title: The Hyphasis Mutiny
sources.quote: Alexander claimed the omens were unfavorable for further advancement into India and so he ended his march.

sources.title: Arrian on the mutiny at the Hyphasis
sources.quote: In the Summer of 326, Alexander's men refused to join their king in his attempt to reach the Ganges valley.

claim: A Hittite prince married a widowed Egyptian queen and was crowned pharaoh in the 14th century BCE.
record: A widowed queen, most often identified as Tutankhamun's wife Ankhesenamun, begged Hittite king Suppiluliuma I for a son: 'To me he will be husband, but in Egypt he will be king.' After months of doubt he sent Prince Zannanza, who died before reaching Egypt. Suppiluliuma blamed the Egyptians; how he died is unknown.

sources.title: Zannanza
sources.quote: His son, Zannanza, was chosen and sent to Egypt to become the new pharaoh. However, the Hittite prince never made it past the Egyptian border, though exactly what became of him and how he died is unknown.

sources.title: Rediscovering Egypt's Golden Dynasty: A Foreign Affair
sources.quote: Only after months of considering the proposal did he eventually send his son Zannanza to Egypt to be wed and crowned pharaoh.

claim: Egypt's Great Pyramid at Giza was built by armies of slaves.
record: Workers' tombs found beside the Giza pyramids since 1990 held builders buried in the king's shadow with jars of bread and beer for the afterlife, a privilege Egyptologists say slaves never had. By one estimate, about 10,000 laborers worked three-month shifts, fed 21 cattle and 23 sheep a day from farms across Egypt.
origin: Herodotus, writing some two thousand years later, told of 100,000 Egyptians forced to toil for an oppressive king in three-month shifts; Hollywood epics later turned that into whip-driven slave gangs.

sources.title: Egypt discovers workers' tombs near pyramids
sources.quote: Graves of the pyramid builders were first discovered in the area in 1990, he said, and discoveries such as these show that the workers were paid laborers, rather than the slaves of popular imagination.

sources.title: Tombs suggest pyramids not built by slaves
sources.quote: The ancient Greek historian, Herodotus, once described the pyramid builders as slaves, creating what Egyptologists say is a myth later propagated by Hollywood films.

sources.title: The History of Herodotus, Vol. 1, Book II (Macaulay translation)
sources.quote: for he shut up all the temples, and having first kept them from sacrificing there, he then bade all the Egyptians work for him.

claim: The Library of Alexandria was wiped out in one great fire during Julius Caesar's war in Egypt in 48 BCE.
record: Caesar's blaze probably burned dockside warehouses and many scrolls, but the institution survived: the geographer Strabo visited its research center around 20 BCE. The Library faded over centuries through purges of scholars, shrinking funds, neglect and crumbling papyrus.
origin: Plutarch wrote that Caesar's fire spread from the docks and destroyed the great library; later writers turned a slow institutional decline into one dramatic blaze.

sources.title: Library of Alexandria
sources.quote: Whatever damage Caesar's fire may have caused, evidently the Library was not completely destroyed.

sources.title: The Real Lesson of the Burning of the Library of Alexandria
sources.quote: The fires were major incidents in which many books were lost, but the institution of the library disappeared more gradually both through organizational neglect and through the gradual obsolescence of the papyrus scrolls themselves.

claim: Ancient Romans built rooms called vomitoria where diners threw up so they could keep on feasting.
record: A vomitorium was a passageway in an amphitheater or stadium that let crowds 'spew forth' into their seats and pour out at the end of a show. The word first appears in Macrobius in the 5th century, and no ancient source uses it for a place to purge.
origin: The Latin root vomere, 'to spew forth,' invited confusion; 19th-century newspapers and Aldous Huxley's comic novel Antic Hay spread the image of Roman purging rooms.

sources.title: Vomitorium
sources.quote: A common misconception about vomitoria is that Ancient Romans had designated spaces called vomitoria for the purpose of literal vomiting, so that they could purge to eat more, after binge eating.

sources.title: Mythbusting Ancient Rome – the truth about the vomitorium
sources.publisher: School of Historical and Philosophical Inquiry, University of Queensland
sources.quote: The vomitorium is clearly part of this group, but no ancient source actually employs the word to describe a place for post-prandial puking.

claim: Julius Caesar was born by caesarean section, and the operation is named after his birth.
record: Roman surgeons cut a baby from the womb only when the mother was dead or dying, yet Caesar's mother Aurelia lived until he was an adult. The operation's name may instead trace to the Latin caedere, 'to cut,' or to a Roman law requiring the surgery.
origin: Pliny the Elder claimed an early ancestor of Caesar's family was 'cut from the womb,' explaining the name Caesar; retellings later transferred the story to Julius himself.

sources.title: Caesarean section
sources.quote: Some popular misconceptions involve Caesar himself being born from the procedure, which is considered false because the procedure was lethal to mothers in ancient Rome, and Caesar's mother Aurelia Cotta lived until he was an adult.

sources.title: Cesarean Section - A Brief History
sources.quote: It is commonly believed to be derived from the surgical birth of Julius Caesar, however this seems unlikely since his mother Aurelia is reputed to have lived to hear of her son's invasion of Britain.

claim: After destroying Carthage in 146 BCE, the Romans sowed its fields with salt so nothing would ever grow there.
record: Rome did raze Carthage, enslave its survivors and forbid anyone to live there, and ten senators ordered whatever remained obliterated. But no ancient writer mentions salt; Appian even notes that simply walking on the site was not forbidden.
origin: The salting shows up in 19th-century reference books, then entered scholarship through B. L. Hallward's chapter in the 1930 Cambridge Ancient History and was long accepted as fact.

sources.title: Salting the earth
sources.quote: Though ancient sources mention symbolically drawing a plow over various cities and salting them, none mention Carthage in particular. The salting story entered the academic literature in Bertrand Hallward's chapter in the first edition of the Cambridge Ancient History (1930), and was widely accepted as factual.

sources.title: Salting the earth
sources.quote: The salting-the-earth story, though, is pure myth. There isn’t a shred of ancient evidence to suggest that it happened.

sources.title: Siege of Carthage (Third Punic War)
sources.quote: the notion that Roman forces then sowed the city with salt is a 19th-century invention.

sources.title: Appian, The Punic Wars 27 (Punica 135)
sources.quote: They decreed that if anything was still left of Carthage, Scipio should obliterate it and that nobody should be allowed to live there. Direful threats were leveled against any who should disobey and chiefly against the rebuilding of Byrsa or Megara, but it was not forbidden to go upon the ground.

claim: Ancient Greek sculptors meant their marble statues to be seen as gleaming, unpainted white stone.
record: Greek statues were painted, with colored eyes, hair and patterned clothing, and traces of pigment survive on well-preserved pieces. Time and weather stripped most of it away. Euripides even has Helen wish she could shed her beauty the way you would wipe color off a statue.
origin: Excavated statues had lost most of their paint, and 18th-century critic Johann Winckelmann hailed white marble as ideal beauty; for generations after, antiquarians who pictured the statues in color were dismissed as eccentrics.

sources.title: True Colors
sources.quote: Colored statues? To us, classical antiquity means white marble. Not so to the Greeks, who thought of their gods in living color and portrayed them that way too.

sources.title: Ancient Greek sculpture
sources.quote: Ancient Greek sculptures were originally painted in multiple colours; they appear colourless today only because the original pigments have deteriorated.

claim: The Soviet Union fired nuclear missiles at the US in 1983 after its satellites reported five incoming ICBMs.
record: Soviet satellites really did flag five American launches on 26 September 1983. Duty officer Stanislav Petrov reasoned a true first strike would be far bigger, waited for radar confirmation that never came and treated it as a false alarm. Sunlight glinting off high clouds had fooled the sensors.

sources.title: 1983 Soviet nuclear false alarm incident
sources.quote: He decided to wait for corroborating evidence—of which none arrived—rather than immediately relaying the warning up the chain of command.

sources.title: The Man Who "Saved the World" Dies at 77
sources.quote: Petrov went with false alarm, later explaining he reasoned that if the United States really were to start a nuclear war, it would do so with more than five missiles.

sources.title: Stanislav Petrov
sources.quote: On 26 September 1983, just three weeks after the Soviet military had shot down Korean Air Lines Flight 007, Lieutenant Colonel Petrov was the duty officer at the command center for the Oko nuclear early-warning system when the system reported that five missiles had been launched from the United States.

claim: A hydrogen bomb exploded over North Carolina in 1961 after falling from a US B-52 that broke apart in mid-air.
record: Two 3.8-megaton Mark 39 bombs fell near Goldsboro. On one, the parachute opened and the arming sequence ran almost to the end; a single low-voltage arm/safe switch, still set to 'safe', blocked the blast. A Sandia engineer later wrote that this one switch stood between the US and catastrophe.

sources.title: 1961 Goldsboro B-52 crash
sources.quote: Parker F. Jones, a supervisor at Sandia, concluded in a reassessment of the accident in 1969 that "one simple, dynamo-technology, low voltage switch stood between the United States and a major catastrophe"

sources.title: Brush with Catastrophe: The Day the U.S. Almost Nuked Itself
sources.quote: One of the bombs performed precisely in accordance with its design: its parachute deployed, its trigger mechanisms engaged, and, remarkably, one single low-voltage switch thwarted unimaginable destruction.

claim: In 1962 the US military staged a fake airliner shootdown to create an excuse for invading Cuba.
record: The Joint Chiefs formally proposed it in Operation Northwoods, a March 1962 memo signed by chairman Lyman Lemnitzer that also floated a 'real or simulated' sinking of a boat of Cuban refugees. Kennedy rejected the scheme, none of it was carried out, and the memo stayed secret until 1997.

sources.title: Operation Northwoods
sources.quote: Although part of the US government's anti-communist Cuban Project, Operation Northwoods was never officially accepted; it was approved by the Joint Chiefs of Staff but then rejected by President Kennedy.

sources.title: Chairman, Joint Chiefs of Staff, Memorandum to the Secretary of Defense, "Justification for US Military Intervention in Cuba," 13 March 1962
sources.publisher: National Security Archive, George Washington University
sources.quote: Of all the Mongoose documents, this one from the Joint Chiefs with the code word “Northwoods” ranks as the most shocking, proposing pretexts like a fake shoot down of a civilian airliner that would justify a U.S. invasion of Cuba.

claim: In 1959 the US Air Force exploded a nuclear bomb on the Moon so that the flash could be seen from Earth.
record: Project A119, a secret 1958 Air Force study, settled on a small W25 warhead and had a young Carl Sagan modelling how the dust cloud would spread. The Air Force cancelled it in January 1959; the plan surfaced only in 1999–2000, via a Sagan biography and project leader Leonard Reiffel.

sources.title: Project A119
sources.quote: The project was canceled by the Air Force in January 1959, seemingly out of fear of the risk to the population if anything went wrong with the launch.

sources.title: Why the Air Force Almost Blasted the Moon with an H-Bomb
sources.quote: Sometime before May 1958, the U.S. Air Force asked the ARF team to investigate something truly out of the ordinary: the visibility and effects of a hypothetical nuclear explosion on the moon.

sources.title: US planned one big nuclear blast for mankind
sources.quote: Reiffel was approached by senior US Air Force officers in 1958, who asked him to 'fast-track' a project to investigate the visibility and effects of a nuclear explosion on the moon.

claim: In the 1960s the US Army hid 600 nuclear missiles in tunnels beneath Greenland's ice sheet.
record: Project Iceworm planned exactly that, and the Army built a nuclear-powered test base, Camp Century, inside the ice, complete with a hospital, theatre and church. But the creeping ice squeezed the tunnels, Denmark never consented, and no Iceworm missiles were ever deployed.

sources.title: Project Iceworm
sources.quote: The missiles, which could strike targets within the Soviet Union, were never fielded and necessary consent from the Danish government to do so was never obtained.

sources.title: Camp Century
sources.publisher: Atomic Heritage Foundation / National Museum of Nuclear Science & History
sources.quote: Although the project was eventually canceled and no missiles were ever deployed to Greenland, it would have been an extraordinary engineering and construction achievement had Iceworm come to fruition.

sources.title: When the Pentagon Dug Ice Tunnels in Greenland to Hide Nukes
sources.quote: Operation Iceworm was shut down because the walls of snow and ice kept moving, squeezing the tracks that carried the missile train.

claim: American and Soviet tanks exchanged fire at Berlin's Checkpoint Charlie in October 1961.
record: On 27 October 1961 US and Soviet tanks faced each other barely 100 yards apart, main guns trained, after a row over Allied access to East Berlin. A back-channel understanding between Kennedy and Khrushchev ended it: the Soviet tanks withdrew the next morning, the Americans followed, and no shots were fired.

sources.title: Berlin Crisis of 1961
sources.quote: A brief stand-off between American and Soviet tanks occurred at Checkpoint Charlie in October after a dispute about free movement of Allied personnel; the confrontation ended peacefully after Khrushchev and Kennedy agreed to withdraw the tanks and reduce tensions.

sources.title: Standoff in Berlin, October 1961
sources.quote: With the attention of the world fixed on Berlin, American and Soviet tanks, barely one hundred yards apart, faced each other for more than 24 hours with their main guns trained on each other.

sources.title: Tanks at Checkpoint Charlie – The Cold War in October 1961
sources.quote: The confrontation at Checkpoint Charlie ended without any shots being fired.

claim: Taiwan secretly built its own atomic bomb in the late 1980s.
record: Taiwan's covert program had completed every stage short of final assembly and testing, reportedly a year or two from a deliverable weapon. Then in January 1988 the CIA spirited out Colonel Chang Hsien-yi, its informant inside the program, and US pressure shut the effort down.

sources.title: Taiwan and weapons of mass destruction
sources.quote: The final secret nuclear weapons program was shut down in the late 1980s under US pressure after completing all stages of weapons development besides final assembly and testing.

sources.title: How a CIA informant stopped Taiwan from developing nuclear weapons
sources.quote: Chang exposed Taiwan’s secret nuclear program to the United States, its closest ally, passing intelligence that ultimately led the US to pressure Taiwan into shutting down the program – which proliferation experts say was near completion.

claim: Russia launched a nuclear strike in 1995 after mistaking a Norwegian science rocket for a US missile.
record: Russian radar read a Black Brant XII rocket, sent up from Norway to study the northern lights, as a possible US Trident missile. Boris Yeltsin was handed the Cheget nuclear briefcase, the only known activation in a crisis, but within minutes officers saw the rocket heading away from Russia.

sources.title: Norwegian rocket incident
sources.quote: The Norwegian rocket incident was the first and thus far only known incident where any nuclear-weapons state had its nuclear briefcase activated and prepared for launching an attack.

sources.title: When Russian Radar Mistook a Norwegian Scientific Rocket for a U.S. Missile, the World Narrowly Avoided Nuclear War
sources.quote: Russian President Boris Yeltsin was notified and given the Cheget, Russia's nuclear briefcase—typically kept near the leader of a nuclear-weapons state at all times.

claim: In the 1960s the CIA surgically fitted a cat with a microphone and radio transmitter to eavesdrop on people.
record: Project Acoustic Kitty put a microphone in a cat's ear canal, a transmitter at the base of its skull and an antenna woven through its fur. Cats proved hard to steer, and a closing memo concluded the idea would not be practical for real intelligence work.

sources.title: Acoustic Kitty
sources.quote: In an hour-long procedure, a veterinary surgeon implanted a microphone in the cat's ear canal, a small radio transmitter at the base of its skull, and a thin wire into its fur.

sources.title: The CIA Experimented On Animals in the 1960s Too. Just Ask 'Acoustic Kitty'
sources.quote: The antenna was made from fine wire and woven, all the way to the tail, through the cat's long fur to conceal it.

claim: In 1962 a US hydrogen bomb exploded 250 miles up in space and knocked out streetlights in Hawaii.
record: The Starfish Prime test above Johnston Atoll unleashed an electromagnetic pulse far bigger than expected, killing about 300 streetlights and tripping burglar alarms roughly 900 miles away in Hawaii. Hotels there had thrown rooftop parties to watch the glowing artificial aurora.

sources.title: Starfish Prime
sources.quote: The Starfish Prime electromagnetic pulse also made those effects known to the public by causing electrical damage in Hawaii, about 900 miles (1,450 km) away from the detonation point, knocking out about 300 streetlights, setting off numerous burglar alarms, and damaging a telephone company microwave link.

sources.title: Going Nuclear Over the Pacific
sources.quote: Telephone service was disrupted, streetlights were down and burglar alarms were set off by a pulse that was much larger than scientists expected.

claim: In 1945 Soviet children gave the US ambassador a carved Great Seal that secretly held a listening bug.
record: Young Pioneers presented the wooden eagle to Averell Harriman as a 'gesture of friendship', and it hung in the ambassador's Moscow residence until the bug was exposed in 1952. Its designer, Leon Theremin, also invented the theremin; the device had no battery and woke only when agents beamed radio waves at it.

sources.title: The Thing (listening device)
sources.quote: On August 4, 1945, several weeks before the end of World War II, a delegation from the Young Pioneer Organization of the Soviet Union presented the bugged carving to Ambassador Harriman, as a "gesture of friendship" to the Soviet Union's war ally.

sources.title: Cold War Espionage Stories: Listening In
sources.publisher: Wright Museum of World War II
sources.quote: In August 1945, as the Allied victory in World War II was rapidly approaching, a group of Soviet students and members of the Young Pioneers presented U.S. Ambassador W. Averell Harriman with a handsome wooden carving of the Great Seal of the United States.

claim: British engineers proposed sealing live chickens inside a 1950s nuclear landmine to keep it warm.
record: Blue Peacock was a ten-kiloton mine meant to be buried in West Germany against a Soviet advance. Fearing its electronics would freeze, designers suggested chickens with a week of food and water as living heaters. The file was released on 1 April 2004, and the National Archives insisted the Civil Service does not do jokes.

sources.title: Blue Peacock
sources.quote: One proposal suggested that live chickens would be sealed inside the casing, with a supply of food and water.

sources.title: In The 1950s, The UK Tried To Make A Nuclear Bomb Filled With Live Chickens
sources.quote: In order to keep the bomb warm and operational, the idea was to take a group of unsuspecting chickens and seal them within the bomb's casing.

claim: Two Soviet tortoises flew around the Moon and back to Earth in 1968, months before any human did.
record: Zond 5 looped around the Moon in September 1968 carrying two Russian tortoises, fruit fly eggs and plants, then splashed down in the Indian Ocean. The tortoises had lost a little weight but were otherwise healthy. Apollo 8's crew circled the Moon that December.

sources.title: Zond 5
sources.quote: In September 1968 Zond 5 travelled around the Moon in a circumlunar trajectory and became the first Moon mission to include animals and the first to return safely to Earth.

sources.title: 50 Years Ago: On the Way to the Moon
sources.quote: Scientists found that the tortoises, the first living organisms to have made a circumlunar flight, had lost a little weight but were otherwise in good health.

claim: In 1966 the US ambassador to Spain swam for the press to show an H-bomb accident hadn't tainted the sea.
record: After a B-52 collision scattered four hydrogen bombs around Palomares, Ambassador Angier Biddle Duke and Spanish minister Manuel Fraga took a much-photographed dip on 8 March. 'If this is radioactivity, I love it!' Duke told reporters, with the last bomb still missing offshore.

sources.title: 1966 Palomares accident
sources.quote: To defuse public alarm over contamination, on 8 March Spanish minister for information and tourism Manuel Fraga Iribarne and United States ambassador Angier Biddle Duke swam on nearby beaches in front of the press.

sources.title: Remembering the Palomares H-bomb Incident via History
sources.publisher: The University of Chicago, Atomic Age blog
sources.quote: On March 8, U.S. Ambassador Angier Biddle Duke even held a much-publicized “swimming party” where he took a dip at one of Palomares’ beaches to prove the water was safe.

claim: NASA spent millions developing a pen that writes in space while Soviet cosmonauts simply used pencils.
record: Paul Fisher spent about $1 million of his own company's money on the pressurized Space Pen, then pitched it to NASA. NASA ordered 400 for Apollo and the Soviets ordered 100 a year later, both paying $2.39 a pen. Pencils were a hazard anyway: flaking tips and flammable wood.
origin: An internet-era joke that hopped from inbox to inbox and even surfaced on The West Wing in 2002; a space historian was heard telling it, pencil held up for the punchline.

sources.title: Fact or Fiction?: NASA Spent Millions to Develop a Pen that Would Write in Space, whereas the Soviet Cosmonauts Used a Pencil
sources.quote: Paul C. Fisher and his company, the Fisher Pen Company, reportedly invested $1 million to create what is now commonly known as the space pen. None of this investment money came from NASA's coffers--the agency only became involved after the pen was dreamed into existence.

sources.title: The billion dollar space pen
sources.quote: This story, like most modern urban legends, has proliferated on the Internet, but it has also been passed by word of mouth.

sources.title: Space Pen
sources.quote: However, the claim that NASA spent millions on the Space Pen is incorrect, as the Fisher pen was developed using private capital, not government funding.

claim: The Moscow–Washington hotline set up in 1963 was a red telephone the US president could pick up.
record: The hotline linked teletype machines, with the American end at the Pentagon, partly because written messages left less room for heated misunderstandings. It switched to fax in 1986 and has run as secure email since 2008. It never carried a phone call.
origin: The 1964 films Fail-Safe and Dr. Strangelove showed hotline telephones, and later TV shows and campaign ads built around a ringing 'red phone' fixed the image.

sources.title: Moscow–Washington hotline
sources.quote: A hotline telephone was depicted in the film Fail-Safe as the "Red 1 / Ultimate 1 Touch phone", and also in Stanley Kubrick's film Dr. Strangelove, both from 1964 and both loosely based on Peter George's Cold War thriller novel Red Alert from 1958.

sources.title: Was there really a "red telephone" hotline during the Cold War?
sources.quote: Rather than a telephone link, which presented the possibility of miscommunications, the hotline consisted of teletype machines that allowed the two countries to send written messages to one another via transatlantic cable.

claim: Berliners laughed at JFK in 1963 because 'Ich bin ein Berliner' meant 'I am a jelly doughnut.'
record: Kennedy's German was correct, and in Berlin the jam doughnut is usually called a Pfannkuchen anyway. The crowd did laugh seconds later, but at his quip thanking the interpreter for translating his German.
origin: Len Deighton's 1983 spy novel Berlin Game joked that a Berliner is a doughnut; a New York Times review repeated it as fact, and a 1988 Times op-ed spread it widely.

sources.title: Ich bin ein Berliner
sources.quote: The misconception appears to have originated in Len Deighton's 1983 spy novel Berlin Game, which contains the following passage, spoken by Bernard Samson:

sources.title: TWE Remembers: John F. Kennedy's "Ich bin ein Berliner" Speech
sources.quote: The legend has persisted despite being debunked time and again, perhaps because so many news sources, including the august New York Times, have repeated the mistake over and over.

claim: NASA developed the orange drink Tang for its astronauts during the 1960s space race.
record: General Foods food scientist William A. Mitchell, who also created Pop Rocks and Cool Whip, formulated Tang in 1957, and it reached shops in 1959. Sales were poor until NASA picked it for John Glenn's 1962 orbital eating experiments.
origin: Tang flew on Gemini and Apollo missions while General Foods ran an advertising blitz on the space link, so most people met the drink through NASA and assumed the agency invented it.

sources.title: Tang (drink mix)
sources.quote: Since then it has been closely associated with the U.S. human spaceflight program, which created the misconception that Tang was invented for the space program.

sources.title: NASA invented Tang? It's a myth
sources.quote: Contrary to popular myth, Tang was NOT invented by NASA. The orange breakfast drink was developed in 1957 by General Foods, but it wasn't used in space until 1962.

sources.title: Advertisement for Tang, "Chosen for the Gemini Astronauts," 1966
sources.quote: General Foods Corporation marketed Tang, a fruit flavored powdered drink, in 1959. Sales were poor until NASA selected it for use on John Glenn's 1962 Mercury flight and subsequent missions.

claim: Several Soviet cosmonauts died on secret space flights before Yuri Gagarin's 1961 orbit.
record: Soviet archives and cosmonaut memoirs opened after 1991 turned up no such flights. What Moscow really hid was a death on the ground: trainee Valentin Bondarenko died after a fire in a test chamber less than three weeks before Gagarin flew.
origin: Late-1950s rumours in the Italian press, then two Turin radio hams, the Judica-Cordiglia brothers, who claimed to have recorded dying cosmonauts; Bondarenko's unexplained vanishing from group photos fed the stories.

sources.title: Lost Cosmonauts
sources.quote: Even with the availability of published Soviet archival material and memoirs of Russian space pioneers, no evidence has emerged to support the Lost Cosmonaut theories.

sources.title: The "Lost Cosmonauts" Theory And The Recording That Claims To Back It Up
sources.quote: No details of lost cosmonauts, or anything that would verify these recordings and other stories, have been found.

sources.title: Valentin Bondarenko
sources.quote: Bondarenko had already appeared in group films and photos of the first cosmonaut group, and his unexplained disappearance sparked rumours of cosmonauts dying in failed launches.

claim: Before leading Cuba's revolution, Fidel Castro was offered a contract to pitch in US Major League Baseball.
record: Castro pitched as a schoolboy, but baseball historian Peter Bjarkman found he never made the University of Havana team and was never a serious big-league prospect. The oft-quoted $5,000 New York Giants bonus rests on scouting reports nobody else has ever seen.
origin: Don Hoak's invented 1964 Sport magazine tale, written with Myron Cope, of batting against a young Castro in Havana fed the legend; a 1989 Harper's piece by David Truby added the Giants and the $5,000 bonus.

sources.title: Fidel Castro and Baseball
sources.quote: Fidel was never a serious pitching prospect who might demand a $5,000 bonus or even a serious contract offer.

sources.title: Review of Fidel Castro and Baseball: The Untold Story
sources.quote: As for the myth, Bjarkman attributed its genesis to an interview of Don Hoak, a former major league baseball player, conducted by journalist Myon Cope, which was published in Sport magazine in June 1964.

claim: In 1892 a Rhode Island family dug up their dead daughter and burned her heart to stop a 'vampire'.
record: When tuberculosis kept killing the Brown family of Exeter, neighbours blamed the dead. Mercy Brown's body was exhumed, her heart burned on a rock, and the ashes mixed into medicine for her dying brother Edwin. He died anyway.

claim: The first jack-o'-lanterns, carved in Ireland and Britain, were hollowed-out pumpkins.
record: In Ireland and Britain, lantern faces were carved into turnips, swedes and mangelwurzels. Pumpkins are native to the Americas and took over the job in North America, where they were bigger and easier to carve.

sources.title: How Jack O'Lanterns Originated in Irish Myth
sources.quote: Immigrants from these countries brought their vegetable-carving traditions with them when they came to the United States

origin: American Halloween imagery made the pumpkin so dominant that people assumed it had always been the vegetable of choice.

claim: Harry Houdini, the escape artist, died on Halloween.
record: Houdini died in Detroit on 31 October 1926 of peritonitis from a ruptured appendix, days after a student punched him in the stomach backstage in Montreal. Séances have been held for him on Halloween ever since.

sources.title: October 31, 1926: Death Proves Inescapable for Even Houdini
sources.quote: But this day in 1926 the Great Houdini was unable to cheat death one more time and succumbed to peritonitis resulting from a ruptured appendix at age 52.

claim: Orson Welles's 1938 radio play 'The War of the Worlds' sent a terrified America fleeing into the streets.
record: Few people were even listening: a ratings survey that night found just 2% of those polled tuned to the play. Some listeners were genuinely frightened, but nothing like a nationwide stampede took place.

sources.title: The War of the Worlds (1938 radio drama)
The Myth of the War of the Worlds Panic
sources.publisher: Slate (Jefferson Pooley and Michael J. Socolow)
sources.quote: In other words, 98 percent of those surveyed were listening to something else, or nothing at all, on Oct. 30, 1938.

origin: Newspapers, losing advertising to radio, splashed isolated reports of fright across front pages, and later retellings treated those stories as proof of a national panic.

claim: Strangers poisoning trick-or-treat candy have killed children across America.
record: Sociologist Joel Best combed decades of news reports and found no confirmed case of a stranger killing a child with poisoned Halloween candy. The notorious 1974 Texas death was caused by the boy's own father, for insurance money.
origin: A few real family crimes and many hoaxes were retold as random attacks by strangers, and the warnings became an annual tradition.

claim: Bram Stoker published his vampire novel with its villain named Count Wampyr.
record: Stoker's working notes call the villain Count Wampyr. Before publication in 1897 he found the name Dracula in a book on Wallachia and used it instead.

sources.title: Dracula Lives! (in Philadelphia)
sources.quote: Stoker originally planned to call his vampire “Count Wampyr” but changed it to “Count Dracula”

claim: Europe's witch hunts executed about nine million people.
record: Modern estimates mostly run from about 40,000 to 60,000 executions in Europe between roughly 1450 and 1750, and even high estimates stay under 100,000. Most took place in the early modern period, not the Middle Ages.

sources.title: Witch trials in the early modern period
Witches: Origins, Wicca, Witch Hunts & Trials
sources.quote: Between the years 1500 and 1660, up to 80,000 suspected witches were put to death in Europe.

origin: The nine-million figure traces to an 18th-century extrapolation by Gottfried Christian Voigt and was repeated by 20th-century writers.

claim: The ancient Celts worshipped a god of the dead named Samhain every 31 October.
record: Samhain was the name of a Gaelic festival marking the end of the harvest season, not a god. No early source mentions a deity called Samhain.

sources.title: Trick or Treat: A History of Halloween (excerpt, Lisa Morton, Reaktion Books)
sources.quote: Vallancey believed this was a 'false derivation', and went on to state that Samhain was actually a Celtic deity who was also known as 'balsab… for Bal is lord, and Sab death'.

origin: The 'Lord of Death' Samhain was invented by 18th-century antiquarians such as Charles Vallancey and spread through later Halloween lore.

claim: In 1954 hundreds of Glasgow children stormed a cemetery hunting a vampire with iron teeth.
record: On 23 September 1954 children armed with sticks and knives searched Glasgow's Southern Necropolis for a 'vampire with iron teeth' said to have eaten two boys. Police cleared them out; there was no vampire, and no missing boys.

claim: A reigning king of Scotland wrote a book on how to hunt witches.
record: James VI of Scotland, later James I of England, published Daemonologie in 1597 after taking part in the North Berwick witch trials. It argued that witchcraft was real and should be punished.

sources.title: The Scottish king who wrote a treatise on demonology and obsessed over witches
sources.quote: A few years later, James decided to write a treatise called Daemonologie, setting out his views on the relationship between witches and their master, the devil.

claim: In Mary Shelley's novel, the monster is named Frankenstein.
record: Frankenstein is Victor Frankenstein, the student who builds the creature. The creature itself is never given a name; the book calls it the creature, the fiend or the daemon.

sources.title: Frankenstein: Penetrating the Secrets of Nature — Transformation of a Monster
sources.quote: Mary Shelley had not given her monster a name; later, audiences would use the word Frankenstein to refer both to the monster and his maker.

origin: Stage versions from 1823 and Universal's films from 1931 made the creature the star, and audiences moved its maker's name onto it.

claim: The first film adaptation of Frankenstein was made by Thomas Edison's film studio.
record: Edison Studios released a 16-minute Frankenstein in 1910, directed by J. Searle Dawley. The monster was created in a vat of chemicals rather than stitched together.

sources.title: Frankenstein (1910)
sources.quote: This was the first filmed version of Frankenstein

claim: In 1876 grave robbers stole Abraham Lincoln's body and held it for ransom.
record: A counterfeiting gang planned to ransom Lincoln's body for the release of their jailed engraver. On election night 1876 they broke into the tomb in Springfield and pried open the sarcophagus, but Secret Service agents tipped off by an informant closed in.

claim: Thieves stole Charlie Chaplin's coffin from a Swiss cemetery and demanded a ransom.
record: In March 1978, two men dug up Chaplin's coffin in Corsier-sur-Vevey and demanded money from his widow. Police traced their calls, arrested them, and found the coffin buried in a nearby field.

sources.title: Grave Robbers Once Held Charlie Chaplin's Body For Ransom
sources.quote: “They said, look, somebody dug up the grave and he's gone,” Chaplin's son Eugene recalled

claim: Vlad the Impaler lived in Transylvania's Bran Castle, sold to tourists today as Dracula's Castle.
record: Vlad III never lived at Bran, which was not under his rule, and his links to it are fleeting at best. Bram Stoker never visited Romania, and there is no evidence he knew of the castle.

sources.title: Visit 'Dracula's Castle' in Transylvania, Romania
sources.quote: Stoker never visited Transylvania, much less Bran Castle.

origin: Twentieth-century tourism promoters attached the Dracula story to a dramatic castle on the old border road.

claim: In 1828 two men in Edinburgh murdered at least 16 people to sell their bodies to an anatomy lecturer.
record: William Burke and William Hare killed their victims and sold the corpses to Dr Robert Knox for his anatomy classes. Hare turned king's evidence; Burke was hanged in 1829 and his own body was publicly dissected.

sources.title: Burke and Hare
sources.publisher: University of Edinburgh, College of Medicine and Veterinary Medicine
sources.quote: Hare escaped by turning King's Evidence against Burke, and Burke was hanged on 28 January, 1829.

claim: Oliver Cromwell's severed head was displayed on a pole above Westminster Hall for more than 20 years.
record: After the monarchy returned, Cromwell's body was dug up and 'executed' in 1661. His head sat on a spike above Westminster Hall until a storm knocked it down in the 1680s. It was finally buried at his old Cambridge college in 1960.

sources.title: Oliver Cromwell's head
sources.quote: on a stormy night in the late 1680s, it was blown from the top of Westminster Hall, thrown to the ground

claim: An admirer dug up Thomas Paine's bones to give him a grand memorial, and then the bones were lost.
record: Radical journalist William Cobbett exhumed Paine in New York in 1819 and shipped the bones to England for a memorial that never happened. After Cobbett's death they passed through several hands and vanished.

claim: Teaching at Oxford University began before the Aztecs founded their capital, Tenochtitlan.
record: There is evidence of teaching at Oxford by 1096, and the university grew rapidly from 1167. The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco in about 1325.

claim: In 1896 Britain and Zanzibar fought a war that lasted less than an hour.
record: On 27 August 1896 British warships shelled the palace of Sultan Khalid bin Barghash after an ultimatum expired. The fighting ended in roughly 38 to 45 minutes, usually called the shortest war on record.

sources.title: Anniversary of the Shortest War in Human History: the Anglo-Zanzibar War
sources.quote: Despite lasting only 38 minutes, the war included an artillery battle and naval action which claimed around 500 lives.

claim: A Japanese soldier kept fighting World War II in the Philippine jungle until 1974.
record: Lieutenant Hiroo Onoda refused to believe the war was over and held out on Lubang Island for 29 years. He surrendered only when his former commanding officer flew out and formally relieved him of duty.

claim: Winston Churchill won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
record: The Swedish Academy awarded Churchill the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature for his historical and biographical writing and his oratory. He never won the Peace Prize.

sources.title: The Nobel Prize in Literature 1953
sources.quote: for his mastery of historical and biographical description as well as for brilliant oratory in defending exalted human values

claim: Nintendo started out in 1889 making playing cards.
record: Fusajiro Yamauchi founded Nintendo Koppai in Kyoto in 1889 to make handmade hanafuda playing cards. Its first home video game machines arrived in 1977, 88 years later.

sources.title: Company History
sources.quote: Fusajiro Yamauchi began manufacturing and selling Japanese playing cards, Hanafuda, in Shimogyo-ku, Kyoto, Japan.

claim: In World War II a brown bear was enlisted in the Polish army, complete with a rank and a service number.
record: Polish soldiers adopted Wojtek as a cub in Iran in 1942 and signed him up so he could travel with them; he ended the war a corporal. Stories of him hauling shell crates at Monte Cassino made him the unit's emblem, though accounts differ on whether the crates were full.

sources.title: Wojtek the Bear: Surprising World War II Animal Hero
sources.quote: The regiment changed its insignia to an image of the bear and an ammo shell and boasted that the bear was an 'enlisted' soldier, giving him a rank and number.

claim: When Skylab fell to Earth, an Australian town fined NASA for littering.
record: Debris from the falling space station landed around Esperance, Western Australia, in July 1979. The shire issued a $400 littering fine, which went unpaid until an American radio host raised the money in 2009.

sources.title: First fine for littering from space
sources.quote: the Shire of Esperance issued NASA with a fine of A$400 for littering

claim: Napoleon Bonaparte was unusually short.
record: Napoleon was about 5 feet 7 inches (1.69 m), average or slightly above for a Frenchman of his time. His height was recorded in French inches, which were longer than English ones.

sources.title: Was Napoleon Short? Origins of the 'Napoleon Complex'
sources.quote: that equals around 1.67 meters, or just under 5'6", which is a little above average for a French man

origin: British caricaturists such as James Gillray drew him tiny, and the confusion between French and English inches made it stick.

claim: Albert Einstein failed mathematics at school.
record: Einstein excelled at maths and had mastered calculus by about 15. He did fail the general section of an entrance exam to the Zurich Polytechnic at 16, while scoring well in maths and physics.

sources.title: Making the Grade - 20 Things You Need to Know About Einstein
sources.quote: In 1935, a rabbi in Princeton showed him a clipping of the Ripley's column with the headline "Greatest living mathematician failed in mathematics." Einstein laughed.

origin: A 'Ripley's Believe It or Not!' column ran the headline 'Greatest living mathematician failed in mathematics'; shown it in 1935, Einstein denied it.

claim: The Great Wall of China can be seen from the Moon with the naked eye.
record: The wall is long but only a few metres wide, roughly the colour of the land around it. It cannot be seen from the Moon, and astronauts in low Earth orbit report it is very hard to see at all without aid.

sources.title: Great Wall
sources.quote: Despite myths to the contrary, the wall isn't visible from the moon, and is difficult or impossible to see from Earth orbit without the high-powered lenses used for this photo.

origin: The idea was in print long before spaceflight, from a 1754 letter by antiquary William Stukeley to a 1932 Ripley's cartoon, and has outlasted Apollo astronauts' reports that no human structure is visible from the Moon.

claim: The Declaration of Independence was signed by the Continental Congress on July 4, 1776.
record: Congress approved the wording on July 4, but most delegates signed the engrossed parchment copy on August 2, 1776. Several signed later still.
origin: July 4 appears on the document and became the celebrated date, so the signing was folded into it. Jefferson and Adams later misremembered it too.

claim: Paul Revere rode through the Massachusetts countryside shouting 'The British are coming!'
record: The ride depended on secrecy, and many colonists still thought of themselves as British. Witnesses recalled the warning as 'The Regulars are coming out.' Revere was also captured before reaching Concord.

sources.title: The Real Story of Paul Revere's Ride
sources.quote: a British patrol intercepted all three men. Prescott and Dawes escaped; Revere was held for some time, questioned, and let go

origin: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's 1860 poem 'Paul Revere's Ride' created the dramatic lone rider the story is remembered by.

claim: Mahatma Gandhi won the Nobel Peace Prize.
record: Gandhi was nominated five times. In 1947 the Nobel committee split three to two against him; after his murder in January 1948 it seriously weighed a posthumous award, then gave no peace prize that year.

sources.title: Mahatma Gandhi, the missing laureate
sources.quote: We know little about the Norwegian Nobel Committee’s discussions on Gandhi’s candidature in 1948 – other than the above quoted entry of November 18 in Gunnar Jahn’s diary – but it seems clear that they seriously considered a posthumous award.

claim: The US Senate removed President Andrew Johnson from office in 1868.
record: The House impeached Johnson, and the Senate voted 35 to 19 to convict him. That was one vote short of the two-thirds needed, so he finished his term.

sources.title: The Impeachment of Andrew Johnson (1868)
sources.quote: A clear majority voted against the president, but the tally fell one vote short of the necessary two-thirds majority to convict.

claim: The crew of Apollo 13 landed on the Moon in April 1970.
record: Apollo 13 was bound for the Fra Mauro highlands when an oxygen tank exploded two days out. The crew swung around the Moon in their lunar module and splashed down safely, without landing.

claim: The Eiffel Tower was pulled down in 1909 when its original 20-year permit ran out.
record: The tower was built for the 1889 Exposition, and Eiffel's permit ran for 20 years. It survived because it proved useful for radio and wireless telegraphy, and the concession was renewed.

sources.title: How the Eiffel Tower Was Saved From Being Demolished
sources.quote: The tower's scientific capabilities led to Eiffel receiving a 70-year extension on his permit

claim: Quebec voted to leave Canada in 1995.
record: On 30 October 1995, Quebecers voted on sovereignty. The No side won by 50.58% to 49.42%, a margin of 54,288 votes out of more than 4.6 million valid ballots, on a turnout of 93.5%.

sources.title: Quebec Referendum (1995)
sources.quote: Ultimately, after an emotional and somewhat controversial campaign, the "No " side achieved victory by a narrow majority of 50.58 per cent.

claim: Aaron Burr was elected president of the United States in 1800.
record: Burr tied Thomas Jefferson with 73 electoral votes each, which threw the election to the House of Representatives. It took 36 ballots in February 1801 before Jefferson won.

sources.title: Electoral College & Indecisive Elections
sources.publisher: US House of Representatives: History, Art & Archives
sources.quote: The 1800 presidential election further tested the presidential selection system when Jefferson and Aaron Burr, the Republican candidates for President and Vice President, tied at 73 electoral ballots each.

claim: In 1976 John Lennon and Paul McCartney reunited the Beatles on live TV for a $3,000 fee.
record: On Saturday Night Live in April 1976, Lorne Michaels offered the Beatles $3,000 to reunite on the show. Lennon and McCartney were watching together at the Dakota and briefly considered heading to the studio, but they decided they were too tired.

claim: In 1859 a bankrupt San Francisco businessman declared himself Emperor of the United States.
record: Joshua Norton proclaimed himself 'Norton I, Emperor of these United States' and later 'Protector of Mexico'. Local businesses honoured his self-printed banknotes, and many thousands of people turned out for his funeral in 1880.

claim: In 1858 the Thames smelled so bad that Parliament rushed through money for London's modern sewers.
record: A hot summer turned the sewage-filled Thames into what the press called the Great Stink. Parliament's river-side curtains were soaked in chloride of lime, and on 2 August a new law let London's Metropolitan Board of Works borrow £3 million for Joseph Bazalgette's sewers.

sources.title: The Great Stink of 1858
sources.quote: Curtains and blinds were soaked in chloride of lime to block the smell. Parliament was sitting that summer, and MPs felt the full force of the stink.

claim: In 1814 a flood of beer from a burst brewery vat killed eight people in London.
record: A 22-foot vat of porter at the Horse Shoe Brewery burst on 17 October 1814, rupturing others. Hundreds of thousands of litres of beer swept into the St Giles slum, demolishing homes; among the dead were mourners at a wake.

sources.title: The London Beer Flood of 1814
sources.quote: On Monday 17th October 1814, a terrible disaster claimed the lives of at least 8 people.

claim: During an 1859 solar storm, some telegraph operators sent messages with their batteries disconnected.
record: The Carrington Event, the strongest geomagnetic storm on record, induced currents in telegraph wires. Operators between Boston and Portland, Maine, unhooked their batteries and kept working on the aurora-driven current alone.

claim: An 18th-century chess-playing 'automaton' that beat Napoleon was secretly operated by a human hidden inside.
record: Wolfgang von Kempelen's Mechanical Turk toured Europe and America for decades and played Napoleon in 1809. A chess master concealed in its cabinet worked the arm through a system of levers and magnets.

claim: A ship stewardess survived the sinking of both the Titanic and her sister ship, the Britannic.
record: Violet Jessop was also aboard the Olympic when it collided with HMS Hawke in 1911. She survived the Titanic in 1912 and the Britannic, sunk by a mine as a hospital ship, in 1916.

sources.title: Servants at Sea: Violet Jessop
sources.quote: She retired at the age of 63 after a 42 year career at sea- surviving the sinking of not one, but two White Star Line ships.

claim: Fanta was invented in wartime Germany when Coca-Cola's German branch couldn't get Coke syrup.
record: Cut off by the wartime trade embargo, Coca-Cola GmbH's head, Max Keith, created a new drink from leftovers such as whey and apple pomace. The name came from 'Fantasie'.

sources.title: Die bewegte Geschichte von Fanta
sources.quote: Im Jahr 1940 ist wegen des zweiten Weltkriegs die Einfuhr des Coca‑Cola Konzentrats in Deutschland verboten und sämtliche Rohstoffe sind knapp.

claim: British intelligence fooled Hitler with fake invasion plans chained to a dead man floated off Spain.
record: The body of a homeless Welshman, dressed as a Royal Marines officer, carried letters pointing to Greece and Sardinia. German intelligence believed them, helping the Allied invasion of Sicily in July 1943.

claim: A US Army unit in World War II used inflatable tanks and sound effects to fake entire divisions.
record: The 23rd Headquarters Special Troops, the 'Ghost Army', staged more than 20 deceptions with rubber tanks, recorded troop noise and fake radio traffic. Many of its members were artists and designers.

sources.title: How the Ghost Army of WWII Used Art to Deceive the Nazis
sources.quote: built on a skeleton of inflatable rubber tubes, covered by rubberized canvas

claim: Russia's Peter the Great made men pay a tax to keep their beards.
record: Returning from western Europe in 1698, Peter wanted a clean-shaven, modern-looking elite. Men who kept their beards paid a yearly fee and carried a token proving it.

sources.title: Why Peter the Great Established a Beard Tax
sources.quote: Those paying the tax were given a token, silver for nobility and copper for commoners.

claim: For over 150 years, England taxed homes by the number of their windows.
record: The window tax began in 1696 as a rough measure of wealth. Owners bricked up windows to pay less, and critics called it a tax on light and air until it was repealed in 1851.

sources.title: The Window Tax: A Case Study in Excess Burden
sources.publisher: Journal of Economic Perspectives (American Economic Association)
sources.quote: In spite of the pernicious health and aesthetic effects and despite widespread protests, the tax persisted for over a century and a half: it was finally repealed in 1851.

claim: Kodak, the film company, built the first self-contained digital camera.
record: Kodak engineer Steven Sasson built a toaster-sized prototype in 1975 that took 23 seconds to record a 0.01-megapixel image onto cassette tape. Kodak kept its film business at the centre and later went bankrupt.

claim: Bubble wrap was first invented as a textured wallpaper.
record: Alfred Fielding and Marc Chavannes sealed two shower curtains together in 1957 hoping to sell textured wallpaper. It flopped, and they later found their market in packaging.

sources.title: The Accidental Invention of Bubble Wrap
sources.quote: They were trying to create a textured wallpaper in 1957 that would appeal to the burgeoning Beat generation

claim: Play-Doh was originally sold as a putty for cleaning soot off wallpaper.
record: Kutol Products made the dough to wipe coal soot from wallpaper. As homes switched to cleaner heating, sales collapsed, and it was relaunched as a children's toy in 1956.

sources.title: The Accidental Invention of Play-Doh
sources.quote: The much-loved children’s toy was a desperate spinoff of a putty used to clean soot off of wallpaper

claim: In the 1830s, pills made from tomato extract were sold in the US as a cure-all.
record: Physician John Cook Bennett touted tomatoes as a remedy for diarrhoea, indigestion and jaundice, and printed recipes for tomato catsup. Patent-medicine makers followed with 'tomato pills', sold with the jingle 'tomato pills will cure all your ills', until the fad collapsed.

sources.title: Tomatoes as Medicine
sources.quote: Meanwhile, Smith notes, other doctors began experimenting with cure-alls made from concentrated forms of tomatoes.

claim: In 2007 a company of Swiss soldiers accidentally marched into Liechtenstein at night.
record: About 170 Swiss infantry recruits lost their way in bad weather and crossed more than a kilometre into Liechtenstein before turning back. Liechtenstein, which has no army, took it in good humour.

claim: For decades Canada and Denmark took turns leaving bottles of liquor on a disputed Arctic island.
record: Military visits to tiny Hans Island between Greenland and Canada became a ritual of planting flags and leaving whisky or schnapps. The dispute ended in 2022 when the island was split between them.

claim: The pathologist who performed Albert Einstein's autopsy removed and kept his brain.
record: Thomas Harvey took the brain during the 1955 autopsy in Princeton, apparently without clear permission, and kept pieces of it for decades, sending samples to researchers.

sources.title: Scientists Get A New Look At Einstein's Brain
sources.quote: In the hours after Einstein's death in 1955, the autopsy pathologist, Thomas Harvey, took dozens of photographs and dissected the physicist's brain into 240 parts for preservation.

claim: In June 1940 Britain and France merged into a single nation with a shared citizenship.
record: With France collapsing, Churchill's cabinet approved a Declaration of Union on 16 June 1940, offering common citizenship and a single war cabinet. Reynaud's ministers, bent on an armistice, met it with hostility; Pétain called it 'fusion with a corpse', and Reynaud resigned that night.

sources.title: June 1940: Britain's forgotten attempt to build a European Union
sources.publisher: LSE British Politics and Policy blog
sources.quote: The declaration was drafted by Jean Monnet, Sir Arthur Salter, and Robert Vansittart, and called for a federal union with joint organs of defence, foreign, financial and economic policies, a common citizenship and a single War Cabinet.

claim: Virgil's Aeneid was burned after his death, as the poet had asked.
record: Dying with the poem unfinished, Virgil asked for the manuscript to be burned. Emperor Augustus overruled the wish and had it published by Virgil's friends Varius and Tucca.

claim: Albert Einstein served as president of Israel.
record: After President Chaim Weizmann died in 1952, Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion's government formally offered Einstein the presidency. He declined, writing that he lacked the aptitude and experience to deal with people.

sources.title: When Albert Einstein Was Asked to Become President of Israel
sources.quote: I am deeply moved by the offer from our State of Israel, and at once saddened and ashamed that I cannot accept it

claim: Britain declared war on Russia in 1904 after the Russian navy fired on British fishing boats.
record: Russia's Baltic Fleet, jumpy on its way to fight Japan, mistook Hull trawlers for Japanese torpedo boats and opened fire, killing two fishermen. Britain ordered its Home Fleet to raise steam, but the crisis ended in an international inquiry and £66,000 in compensation.

sources.title: M2626 | Maritime Memorials (Dogger Bank Incident memorial, Hessle Road, Hull)
sources.quote: TO THE MEMORY OF / GEORGE HENRY SMITH / (SKIPPER) / AND / WILLIAM RICHARD LEGGETT / (THIRD HAND)/OF THE ILL-FATED TRAWLER 'CRANE' / WHO LOST THEIR LIVES IN THE NORTH SEA / BY THE ACTION OF THE RUSSIAN BALTIC FLEET / OCTOBER 22ND 1904

claim: President Ulysses S. Grant annexed the Dominican Republic as US territory in 1870.
record: Grant's government signed an annexation treaty with the Dominican government, but the Senate rejected it in June 1870 on a 28 to 28 vote, far short of the two-thirds needed.

sources.title: An Overlooked Success: How the Failed Annexation of Santo Domingo led to the Successful Prosecution of the Ku Klux Klan
sources.publisher: Not Even Past (University of Texas at Austin, Department of History)
sources.quote: The treaty for the annexation of the island of San Domingo to the United States was rejected by the Senate this afternoon by a vote of 28 to 28, being ten less than the required two-thirds to secure its ratification.

claim: Mount Rushmore's four presidents were carved from the head down to the waist.
record: Sculptor Gutzon Borglum's design showed the presidents to the waist. After Borglum died in March 1941 and funding ran out, work stopped with the faces.

claim: London built a tower taller than the Eiffel Tower at Wembley in the 1890s.
record: Railway magnate Edward Watkin planned a tower to top Eiffel's. Only the first stage, about 47 metres, was finished before money and the sinking ground ran out; it was demolished in 1907, and Wembley Stadium later rose on the site.

claim: Leonardo da Vinci cast a colossal bronze horse for the Duke of Milan.
record: Leonardo made a full-size clay model more than 7 metres tall, but in 1494 the bronze set aside for it was used to make cannons. French soldiers later used the clay model for target practice.

sources.title: Leonardo's Horse: A Long Shot Pays Off
sources.quote: But then a French army threatened and the metal was needed for cannon. When Milan fell in September 1499, Leonardo fled. French archers used the clay horse for target practice.

claim: Blockbuster bought Netflix for $50 million in 2000.
record: Netflix's founders offered to sell to Blockbuster for about $50 million in 2000 and were turned down. Netflix went on to outgrow the video chain, which filed for bankruptcy in 2010.

sources.title: Netflix cofounder Marc Randolph recalls Blockbuster rejecting chance to buy it
sources.quote: In 2000, the two tried to sell their startup to Blockbuster for $50 million. They were flat-out rejected.

claim: The web portal Excite bought Google for $750,000 in 1999.
record: Google's founders first offered Excite their search engine for $1 million in 1999. Investor Vinod Khosla haggled them down to about $750,000, but chief executive George Bell still turned it down.

sources.title: History of Google
sources.quote: Vinod Khosla...talked the duo down to $750,000, but Bell still rejected it

claim: The League of Nations formally recommended that schools around the world teach Esperanto.
record: In September 1922 the League of Nations Assembly adopted a resolution recommending that member states teach Esperanto in schools. French delegate Gabriel Hanotaux had fought recognition for years; France retaliated by banning Esperanto lessons in its own schools.

sources.title: Esperanto as an international auxiliary language. Report of the general Secretariat of the League of Nations adopted by the third Assembly, 1922
sources.publisher: League of Nations / UN Archives Geneva
sources.quote: Resolutions adopted by the Assembly, 21 September 1922

claim: The US Constitution was amended in 1810 to strip citizenship from anyone who accepted a foreign noble title.
record: The Titles of Nobility Amendment passed both houses of Congress in 1810 and went to the states. Between 1812 and 1816 it twice came within two states of ratification, and with no deadline set, it technically remains pending.

sources.title: Unratified Amendments: Titles of Nobility
sources.quote: The amendment was then sent to the state legislatures for ratification but never reached the three-fourths threshold to be added to the Constitution.

claim: Tom Selleck starred as Indiana Jones in Raiders of the Lost Ark.
record: Selleck was chosen for the role, but CBS would not release him from his contract for the new series Magnum, P.I. Harrison Ford was cast instead.

sources.title: Tom Selleck talks losing 'Indiana Jones' role due to 'Magnum, P.I.'
sources.quote: I was offered the role and wanted it, but I had done a pilot of 'Magnum.' And Steven Spielberg and George Lucas kept the offer out to me. They said, 'We'll work it out and you can do both.' And the more they wanted me, the more CBS said, 'No, we don't want to let him do it.'

claim: Decca Records signed the Beatles after their 1962 audition in London.
record: The Beatles auditioned at Decca on 1 January 1962 and were turned down; the label signed Brian Poole and the Tremeloes instead. EMI's Parlophone signed the Beatles later that year.

claim: Kublai Khan's Mongol fleet conquered Japan in 1281.
record: The second Mongol invasion was one of the largest seaborne attacks in history. Stiff Japanese defences held the landings, and a typhoon then wrecked much of the fleet, the storm later remembered as the kamikaze, or divine wind.

sources.title: Japan's Kamikaze Winds, the Stuff of Legend, May Have Been Real
sources.quote: Twice, in 1274 and 1281, Kublai sent his overwhelming forces across the Korea Strait, and twice his fleet was destroyed

claim: The Ottoman army captured Vienna in 1683.
record: After a two-month siege the city's walls were close to breaking. On 12 September 1683 a relief army under the Polish king Jan III Sobieski routed the besiegers.

sources.title: The Period of the Turkish Sieges (1529 to 1683)
sources.quote: The city walls as well as individual buildings in the inner city suffered severe damage.

claim: An assassin shot and killed president-elect Franklin D. Roosevelt in Miami in 1933.
record: Giuseppe Zangara fired five shots at Roosevelt's open car in February 1933. Roosevelt was unhurt, but Chicago mayor Anton Cermak was fatally wounded.

sources.title: Attempted assassination of Franklin D. Roosevelt
Assassination Attempt Lead Bullet Fragment in Case
