sources.quote: Though a bystander deflected his hand, Zangara wounded four people and fatally shot Chicago Mayor Anton Cermak, who was standing beside Roosevelt's car.

claim: Bartholdi's giant robed woman holding a torch was first erected at the entrance to Egypt's Suez Canal.
record: Bartholdi pitched a colossal lighthouse figure, 'Egypt Carrying the Light to Asia', to the Khedive of Egypt around 1869. The Khedive declined, and Bartholdi's later statue went to New York.

claim: The board game Monopoly was invented by Charles Darrow during the Great Depression.
record: Monopoly grew from The Landlord's Game, patented by Lizzie Magie in 1904 to show the evils of land monopolies. Darrow sold a version to Parker Brothers in 1935.

sources.title: Monopoly Was Designed to Teach the 99% About Income Inequality
sources.quote: It was a Quaker iteration that Darrow copied and sold to Parker Brothers in 1935

origin: Parker Brothers' packaging and publicity told Darrow's rags-to-riches story for decades.

claim: Coca-Cola's advertising gave Santa Claus his red suit.
record: Santa wore red and white on Puck magazine covers in the early 1900s, and a mineral-water firm used him in colour ads in the 1920s. Haddon Sundblom's Coca-Cola Santas, from 1931, fixed a warm, human-sized Santa in the public mind.

sources.title: Haddon Sundblom and the Coca-Cola Santas
sources.quote: Nast continued to draw Santa for 30 years, changing the color of his coat from tan to the red he’s known for today.

origin: Coca-Cola's famous and long-running campaign made its Santa the one everyone remembered.

claim: Fortune cookies come from China.
record: Fortune cookies were popularized in California in the early 20th century, most likely by Japanese immigrants adapting a Japanese cracker. They are rare in China.

sources.title: Cracking Open the History of Fortune Cookies
sources.quote: Chinese entrepreneurs stepped in to fill the void and by the end of the war they were indelibly associated with fortune cookies, whose popularity had spread nationwide.

origin: Chinese restaurants in the US adopted them in the mid-20th century, so diners assumed they were Chinese.

claim: Caesar salad is named after Julius Caesar.
record: The salad is credited to Caesar Cardini, an Italian-born restaurateur who served it in Tijuana, Mexico, in the 1920s.
origin: The name is the obvious guess; the restaurateur was named Caesar too.

claim: The croissant was invented in Vienna to celebrate beating the Ottoman siege of 1683.
record: Crescent-shaped kipferl pastries existed in Austria long before 1683, and the flaky croissant was developed in France in the 19th century. No contemporary record ties either to the siege.

sources.title: Is the Croissant Really French?
sources.quote: the kipfel existed long before the Ottoman siege of Vienna

origin: A 20th-century story, repeated in food writing, gave the pastry a heroic origin to match its crescent shape.

claim: Eating carrots gave RAF pilots exceptional night vision during World War II.
record: RAF night fighters were finding German bombers with new airborne radar. British publicity credited carrots instead, possibly partly to mask the radar, while the Ministry of Food pushed a plentiful vegetable. Vitamin A only helps night vision in people who are deficient.

sources.title: A WWII Propaganda Campaign Popularized the Myth That Carrots Help You See in the Dark
sources.quote: Though the British were “happy to go along with the story [of carrot-improved vision], they never set out to use it to fool the Germans,” Legate told Scientific American in 2014.

origin: Wartime British publicity about night-fighter ace John Cunningham and carrot-eating spread the idea.

claim: Potato chips were invented by a Saratoga Springs chef to spite a customer who sent back his fries.
record: Recipes for thin fried potato slices appeared decades earlier, including William Kitchiner's in 1817, and a Saratoga cook named Eliza was famous for her fried potatoes by 1849. Crum's name was not linked to the dish until 1885.

sources.title: The Story of the Invention of the Potato Chip Is a Myth
sources.quote: In almost all its particulars, the story of George Crum's deep-fried stunt is wrong.

origin: The prickly-customer tale grew with retelling, and a 1970s paper-company advertisement cast Cornelius Vanderbilt as the diner, though he was in Europe that summer.

claim: Walt Disney's body was cryogenically frozen after his death.
record: Disney was cremated two days after he died in December 1966, and his ashes were interred at Forest Lawn in Glendale, California.
origin: The rumour spread in the late 1960s alongside public interest in cryonics and Disney's reputation for futurism.

claim: Antonio Salieri poisoned Mozart out of jealousy.
record: There is no evidence Salieri harmed Mozart; the two were professional rivals who also collaborated. Mozart's death is usually attributed to illness.

sources.title: Salieri & the Poisoning of Mozart
sources.quote: Although this is my final illness, I can say in good faith that there is no truth to the absurd rumor that I poisoned Mozart

origin: Rumours after Mozart's death were dramatized by Pushkin in 1830, then by Peter Shaffer's play and film 'Amadeus'.

claim: Medieval jailers tortured prisoners inside the spiked cabinet known as the iron maiden.
record: There is no evidence of iron maidens before the 19th century. The examples shown in museums were pieced together then, often from unrelated old parts, for exhibitions and showmen.

sources.title: 7 Famous Torture Devices, Real and Mythical
sources.quote: The first known iron maidens were constructed in the 19th century, and passed off in museums as medieval torture devices.

origin: Johann Philipp Siebenkees's late-18th-century tale of a 1515 execution in Nuremberg, which historians suspect he invented, launched the legend.

claim: Dr Joseph-Ignace Guillotin was executed by the guillotine he helped create.
record: Guillotin proposed a more humane method of execution but did not invent the machine, and he died of natural causes in Paris in 1814.

sources.title: French history myths: The inventor of guillotine was guillotined
sources.quote: During the Terror a doctor with a similar name was guillotined in Lyon, giving rise to the belief that Joseph-Ignace suffered this ironic death.

origin: A different Dr Guillotin from Lyon was executed during the Revolution, and the coincidence fed the story.

claim: Grand Duchess Anastasia escaped the execution of Russia's royal family and lived on in secret.
record: DNA analysis of remains found near Yekaterinburg, including a second grave discovered in 2007, confirmed that all of Nicholas II's children died with their parents in July 1918.

sources.title: Grand Duchess Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia

origin: Several claimants, most famously Anna Anderson, insisted they were Anastasia; DNA tests later showed Anderson was not.

claim: Tulip mania wrecked the Dutch economy when the bulb bubble burst in 1637.
record: Historians such as Anne Goldgar found little evidence of widespread ruin. The trade involved a fairly small circle of merchants and artisans, and the Dutch economy kept booming.

sources.title: There Never Was a Real Tulip Fever
sources.quote: There weren't that many people involved and the economic repercussions were pretty minor

origin: Moralizing pamphlets of the time and Charles Mackay's 1841 book 'Extraordinary Popular Delusions' magnified the crash.

claim: In 1325 two Italian cities went to war over a stolen wooden bucket.
record: Modena and Bologna fought the Battle of Zappolino as part of a long feud between rival factions. The famous oak bucket was taken as a trophy after the battle, not the cause of it.

sources.title: Palazzo Comunale di Modena
sources.quote: the Secchia rapita (Stolen Bucket), a normal wooden bucket, reminding the people of Modena of their glorious victory against the Bolognese in 1325 in the battle of Zappolino.

origin: Alessandro Tassoni's 1622 mock-epic poem 'The Rape of the Bucket' made the bucket the star of the story.

claim: King Cnut ordered the tide to go back because he believed he could command the sea.
record: In the earliest version, written by Henry of Huntingdon in the 12th century, Cnut lets the tide soak him to prove that a king's power is 'empty and worthless' beside God's. He then hung his gold crown on a crucifix and never wore it again.
origin: The moral got flipped in retelling, turning a lesson in humility into an example of royal arrogance.

claim: Julius Caesar's last words were 'Et tu, Brute?'
record: Ancient writers disagree: Suetonius says Caesar said nothing, or possibly the Greek 'You too, child?'. The Latin line was made famous by Shakespeare's play, written more than 1,600 years later.
origin: Shakespeare's 'Julius Caesar' (1599) gave the moment its famous Latin line.

claim: Voltaire wrote, 'I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it.'
record: The line was written in 1906 by Evelyn Beatrice Hall, in a biography of Voltaire, as a summary of his attitude. It is not found in Voltaire's own writings.

sources.title: Quote Origin: I Disapprove of What You Say, But I Will Defend to the Death Your Right to Say It
sources.quote: is my own expression and should not have been put in inverted commas

origin: Readers took Hall's paraphrase as a direct quotation, and she later had to explain it wasn't.

claim: Armoured medieval knights were so weighed down that they had to be hoisted onto their horses by crane.
record: A full suit of field armour weighed roughly 15 to 25 kilograms, spread across the body. Knights could mount a horse, run and even do acrobatics in it.

sources.title: Debunking the biggest myths about knight's armour
sources.quote: Mann was horrified to discover that his insights and expertise had been ignored, particularly during a scene in which Olivier’s Henry V is lifted onto his noble steed using a crane-like contraption.

origin: Heavier jousting armour and a scene in the 1944 film 'Henry V' helped create the image of a helpless knight on a winch.

claim: Theodore Roosevelt was shot in the chest in 1912 and then gave his campaign speech anyway.
record: In Milwaukee on 14 October 1912, a bullet slowed by his folded 50-page speech and steel glasses case lodged in Roosevelt's chest muscle. He delivered the speech anyway, for somewhere between 50 and 90 minutes depending on the account, before going to hospital.

sources.title: The Speech That Saved Teddy Roosevelt's Life
sources.quote: the bullet had been slowed by the thick manuscript and the spectacles case.

claim: The brother of Lincoln's assassin once saved Lincoln's son from being crushed by a train.
record: On a crowded platform in Jersey City, Robert Todd Lincoln slipped toward a moving train and was pulled back by his collar. His rescuer was the famous actor Edwin Booth, brother of John Wilkes Booth.

claim: John Adams and Thomas Jefferson died on the same day: July 4, 1826, the Declaration's 50th anniversary.
record: Jefferson died at Monticello around midday; Adams died hours later in Massachusetts, reportedly saying 'Thomas Jefferson survives', not knowing his old rival had already died.

sources.title: Thomas Jefferson and John Adams die
sources.quote: His last words were, 'Thomas Jefferson still survives.' He was mistaken: Jefferson had died five hours earlier

claim: James Monroe, the fifth US president, also died on the Fourth of July.
record: Monroe died in New York City on July 4, 1831, five years to the day after Adams and Jefferson. He was the third of the first five presidents to die on Independence Day.

sources.title: James Monroe: Life After the Presidency
sources.quote: He died that year on July 4, in New York City. Monroe was the third of the first five Presidents to die on the Fourth of July

claim: William Henry Harrison died 31 days after giving the longest inaugural address in US history.
record: Harrison read his 8,445-word address for nearly two hours on 4 March 1841, in a cold wind and without an overcoat, and died on 4 April. His death was long blamed on that raw day; a 2014 analysis argued enteric fever from Washington's tainted water was likelier.

sources.title: Science Rewrites the Death of America's Shortest-Serving President
sources.quote: Harrison likely developed enteric fever, and that it was this, not pneumonia, that killed him.

claim: In the 1930s the US Army drew up plans for invading Canada.
record: War Plan Red, approved in 1930 and updated into the 1930s, imagined a war with the British Empire and included seizing Halifax and Canadian rail hubs. It was a planning exercise, and it was declassified in 1974.

claim: In 1921 Canada drew up a plan to invade the United States.
record: Colonel James Sutherland Brown's Defence Scheme No. 1 proposed quick raids into Seattle, Minneapolis and Albany to buy time for British reinforcements. It was shelved in 1928.

sources.title: Invasion plans
sources.quote: It was more than just a thought experiment

claim: Vermont spent 14 years as an unrecognized independent state, with its own coins, before joining the US.
record: Vermont declared independence in January 1777 and, with no recognition from Congress or any foreign power, ran its own government, coinage and postal service. It became the 14th state on 4 March 1791.

sources.title: Discover and Learn | Vermont's 250th
sources.quote: Vermont remained a sovereign republic for fourteen years until January 1791, when it became the first state to join the Union following the ratification of the United States Constitution.

claim: In 1947 engineers taped a real moth into their logbook as the 'first actual case of bug being found'.
record: Operators of Harvard's Mark II computer found a moth stuck in a relay and taped it into the log. Engineers had already called glitches 'bugs', which is why the note is a joke.

sources.title: September 9: First Instance of Actual Computer Bug Being Found
sources.quote: a moth caught between the relay contacts of the Harvard Mark II computer in Cambridge, Massachusetts. They taped the dead moth into the logbook for the computer.

claim: Apollo 12 was struck by lightning twice during its launch and still went on to the Moon.
record: Seconds after liftoff in November 1969, lightning knocked out the command module's instruments. Controller John Aaron's call to switch 'SCE to Aux' restored the data, and the crew landed on the Moon days later.

claim: A cosmonaut left Earth as a Soviet citizen and came home after the Soviet Union had ceased to exist.
record: Sergei Krikalev launched to the Mir station in May 1991. While he was in orbit the USSR dissolved, and he landed in March 1992 as a citizen of Russia.

sources.title: Sergei K. Krikalev
sources.publisher: New Mexico Museum of Space History
sources.quote: On May 18, 1991, Sergei Krikalev returned to Mir as part of the Mir EO-9 crew

claim: In 1978 a Soviet nuclear-powered satellite crashed in Canada and scattered radioactive debris.
record: Kosmos 954, powered by an onboard nuclear reactor, broke up over the Northwest Territories in January 1978. Canada billed the Soviet Union for the clean-up and received about C$3 million.

sources.title: Previous nuclear incidents and accidents: COSMOS 954
sources.quote: On 24 January 1978, COSMOS 954, a Soviet nuclear-powered surveillance satellite, crashed in the Northwest Territories.

claim: NASA lost a Mars probe because one team used English units and another used metric.
record: Software from a contractor reported thruster data in pound-force seconds while NASA's system expected newton-seconds. The Mars Climate Orbiter flew too low and was lost in September 1999.

sources.title: Mars Climate Orbiter
sources.quote: unsuccessful due to a navigation error caused by a failure to translate English units to metric

claim: Chinese treasure fleets reached the coast of East Africa in the 1400s.
record: Admiral Zheng He led seven Ming voyages across the Indian Ocean. Ships from the fleets reached Malindi and Mogadishu, and a giraffe was brought back to the emperor's court.

claim: A West African king gave away so much gold in Cairo that he depressed its value for years.
record: Mansa Musa of Mali passed through Cairo on pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324. According to the chronicler al-Umari, his lavish spending and gifts drove down the value of gold there for about 12 years.

sources.title: Al-Umari's Account of Mansa Musa's Visit to Cairo
sources.quote: They exchanged gold until they depressed its value in Egypt and caused its price to fall

claim: Norse explorers built a settlement in North America about 500 years before Columbus.
record: Excavations at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland uncovered Norse buildings and artefacts. Tree-ring dating of cut wood places activity there in 1021.

sources.title: L'Anse aux Meadows National Historic Site
sources.quote: Here Norse expeditions sailed from Greenland, building a small encampment of timber-and-sod buildings over 1000 years ago

claim: Cleopatra was the first ruler of her dynasty known to have learned the Egyptian language.
record: The Ptolemies were Macedonian Greeks who ruled Egypt for nearly three centuries. According to Plutarch, Cleopatra VII was the first of them to learn Egyptian, among many languages she spoke.

sources.title: Plutarch, Life of Antony, 27 (trans. Bernadotte Perrin, Loeb Classical Library)
sources.quote: although the kings of Egypt before her had not even made an effort to learn the native language, and some actually gave up their Macedonian dialect.

claim: In medieval France a pig was tried in court, convicted of killing a child and executed.
record: Animal trials were a real legal practice. In Falaise in 1386 a sow that had killed an infant was reportedly dressed in clothes and hanged in the town square.

claim: The Olympics once awarded medals for painting, music and literature.
record: Art competitions ran from 1912 to 1948, with medals for architecture, literature, music, painting and sculpture inspired by sport. They were dropped because most entrants were professionals.

sources.title: Art competitions at the Summer Olympics
When the Olympics Gave Out Medals for Art
sources.quote: From 1912 to 1952, juries awarded a total of 151 medals to original works in the fine arts inspired by athletic endeavors

claim: Tug of war was an Olympic sport.
record: Tug of war was part of the Summer Olympics from 1900 to 1920. The City of London Police team won gold twice.

sources.title: Tug of war at the Summer Olympics

claim: The winner of the 1904 Olympic marathon was dosed with rat poison during the race.
record: Thomas Hicks's handlers gave him strychnine mixed with brandy and egg whites as a stimulant, then legal. He had to be held up across the finish line; the first man home had ridden part of the course in a car.

sources.title: Athletics at the 1904 Summer Olympics – Men%27s marathon
How the 1904 Marathon Became One of the Weirdest Olympic Events of All Time
sources.quote: Seven miles from the finish, his handlers fed him a concoction of strychnine and egg whites—the first recorded instance of drug use in the modern Olympics

claim: In 1618 angry nobles threw three officials out of a Prague castle window, and all three survived.
record: Two Catholic regents and their secretary fell some 20 metres into the moat. Catholics credited angels; Protestants said they landed in a dung heap. The incident helped trigger the Thirty Years' War.

claim: Isaac Newton lost a large sum in the South Sea Bubble of 1720.
record: Newton sold early at a profit, then bought back in near the peak and lost heavily when the South Sea Company's shares collapsed. Contemporary accounts put his loss in the thousands of pounds.

sources.title: The Market Crash That Cost Newton a Fortune
sources.quote: Newton jumped back in at a much higher price—and lost £20,000 (or more than $3 million in today's money)

claim: Isaac Newton became a Royal Mint official who personally hunted down counterfeiters.
record: As Warden of the Royal Mint from 1696, Newton oversaw a great recoinage and conducted more than 100 cross-examinations of witnesses, informers and suspects. He prosecuted 28 coiners, including William Chaloner, hanged in 1699.

sources.title: Isaac Newton
sources.quote: The enormous operation was completed within three years, leaving Newton more time to devote to his main duty of investigating and bringing to justice those who clipped and counterfeited the coin of the realm.

claim: The man who pioneered the lobotomy won a Nobel Prize for it.
record: Portuguese neurologist Egas Moniz shared the 1949 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the procedure. It was later largely abandoned as its harms became clear.

claim: In 1958 a US bomber accidentally dropped an atomic bomb on a family's garden in South Carolina.
record: A Mark 6 bomb fell from a B-47 over Mars Bluff. Its nuclear core was not installed, but its conventional explosives blew a crater about 20 metres wide and injured several members of the Gregg family.

sources.title: 1958 Mars Bluff B-47 nuclear weapon loss incident
When the U.S. Air Force Accidentally Dropped an Atomic Bomb on Mars Bluff, South Carolina
sources.quote: a massive crater over 50 feet wide and 30 feet deep

claim: In 1917 Germany secretly offered to help Mexico win back Texas, New Mexico and Arizona.
record: The Zimmermann Telegram proposed an alliance if the US entered World War I. British codebreakers intercepted it, and its publication helped bring America into the war.

sources.title: The Zimmermann Telegram
sources.quote: In January 1917, British cryptographers deciphered a telegram from German Foreign Minister Arthur Zimmermann to the German Minister to Mexico, Heinrich von Eckhardt, offering United States territory to Mexico in return for joining the German cause.

claim: The United States bought what are now the US Virgin Islands from Denmark for $25 million in gold.
record: Worried that Germany might seize the islands as a U-boat base, the US bought St Croix, St John and St Thomas from Denmark, which handed them over on 31 March 1917.

sources.title: Transfer Day, a Significant Day in Virgin Islands History
sources.quote: the United States agreed to purchase the Virgin Islands from a financially strapped Denmark for $25 million in gold coin

claim: A Japanese balloon bomb killed six people on a picnic in Oregon in 1945.
record: Japan launched thousands of hydrogen balloons carrying bombs on the jet stream toward North America. On 5 May 1945 one exploded near Bly, Oregon, killing a pregnant woman and five children.

claim: Some of the ashes of the man who designed the Pringles can were buried in a Pringles can.
record: Fredric Baur, the Procter & Gamble chemist who designed the stackable can, died in 2008. His family honoured his request and buried part of his ashes in one.

sources.title: Man's Final Resting Place: A Pringles Can
sources.quote: Baur's children said they honored his request to bury him in one of the cans by placing part of his cremated remains in a Pringles container in his grave

claim: Apple's third co-founder sold his 10 percent stake back for $800.
record: Ronald Wayne drew up Apple's partnership agreement with Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak and designed its first logo. Twelve days later he withdrew, fearing the financial risk.

claim: In 1698 Scotland tried to found its own colony in Panama.
record: The Darien scheme sank a large share of Scotland's available capital into a colony called New Caledonia. Disease, poor planning and Spanish opposition destroyed it, and the losses helped push Scotland toward union with England in 1707.

claim: The Pony Express mail service operated for only about 18 months.
record: Riders relayed mail between Missouri and California from April 1860 to October 1861. The transcontinental telegraph made it obsolete almost immediately.

claim: Gerald Ford became US president without ever being elected president or vice president.
record: Ford was appointed vice president under the 25th Amendment after Spiro Agnew resigned in 1973, then became president when Richard Nixon resigned in August 1974. He lost the 1976 election.

sources.title: The Unelected President
sources.quote: the only person to serve as President without having been elected to either the vice presidency or the presidency

claim: British troops burned the White House during the War of 1812.
record: On 24 August 1814 British forces occupied Washington and set fire to the President's House, the Capitol and other public buildings. Before fleeing, Dolley Madison ordered Gilbert Stuart's portrait of George Washington taken down and sent to safety.

sources.title: Who saved the Gilbert Stuart painting of George Washington from the White House before it was burned in 1814?
sources.quote: First Lady Dolley Madison ordered the Washington painting to be saved, and it was taken down off the wall and sent out of harm’s way by a group of individuals--Jean Pierre Sioussat, the White House steward; Paul Jennings, an enslaved worker; Thomas McGrath, the White House gardener; and two men from New York

claim: In 1962 an outbreak of uncontrollable laughter forced schools to close in Tanganyika.
record: It began at a girls' boarding school in Kashasha and spread to villages over months, affecting around a thousand people. Researchers describe it as mass psychogenic illness.

claim: During Strasbourg's dancing plague of 1518, the city hired musicians to keep the dancers going.
record: Hundreds of people danced compulsively for weeks. Believing the dancers had to dance it out, the council opened guildhalls, built a stage and paid musicians, before changing course and sending sufferers to a shrine.

claim: Max Brod burned Franz Kafka's unpublished novels, as Kafka had instructed.
record: Kafka left written instructions for his friend to destroy his manuscripts unread. Brod refused and published 'The Trial', 'The Castle' and 'Amerika' after Kafka's death in 1924.

sources.title: Kafka: Metamorphosis of an Author
sources.quote: should be burned without exception and without their being read

claim: American troops captured Quebec City on the last night of 1775.
record: Richard Montgomery and Benedict Arnold attacked through a blizzard on 31 December 1775. Daniel Morgan's men broke through a barricade in the Lower Town, but Montgomery was killed, Arnold wounded and more than 400 Americans captured.

sources.title: Quebec (Battle of Quebec, 1775)
sources.quote: Finally, at around 9 am, General Morgan and over 400 Americans surrendered and were taken prisoner by the British.

claim: The House of Representatives impeached Richard Nixon in 1974.
record: The House Judiciary Committee approved three articles of impeachment in July 1974. Nixon resigned on 9 August before the full House could vote.

sources.title: Impeachment Inquiries into President Richard Nixon
sources.publisher: US House of Representatives: History, Art & Archives
sources.quote: Nixon resigned on August 9 before the full House had an opportunity to vote on the articles.

claim: President Nixon went on television in 1969 to mourn the Apollo 11 astronauts, stranded on the Moon.
record: Speechwriter William Safire wrote 'In Event of Moon Disaster' in case Armstrong and Aldrin could not lift off: 'Fate has ordained that the men who went to the Moon to explore in peace will stay on the Moon to rest in peace.' It was never needed.

claim: Guy Fawkes and his fellow plotters blew up the House of Lords in 1605.
record: Plotters packed 36 barrels of gunpowder into a cellar beneath the Lords, aiming to kill James I at the opening of Parliament. An anonymous warning letter led to a search, and Fawkes was arrested guarding the powder.

claim: A carpenter's time bomb killed Hitler in a Munich beer hall in 1939.
record: Georg Elser spent weeks hollowing out a pillar behind the speaker's podium. Hitler cut his speech short to catch a train and left 13 minutes before the bomb exploded, killing eight people.

sources.title: Georg Elser and the Assassination Attempt of November 8, 1939
sources.quote: On November 8, 1939, Hitler left the assembly room unexpectedly only minutes before the explosion, and thus evaded the assassination attempt.

claim: Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg's briefcase bomb killed Hitler in July 1944.
record: The bomb exploded at the Wolf's Lair on 20 July 1944, but the briefcase had been moved behind a heavy table leg. Hitler was only lightly injured, and the conspirators were hunted down.

sources.title: The July 20, 1944, Plot to Assassinate Adolf Hitler
sources.publisher: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, Holocaust Encyclopedia
sources.quote: It detonated, but failed to kill Hitler.

claim: The Spanish Armada landed an invasion army in England in 1588.
record: The Armada was meant to escort the Duke of Parma's army across from Flanders. English fireships and attacks off Gravelines scattered it, and storms wrecked many ships on the way home.

claim: Australia voted to become a republic in 1999.
record: A referendum proposed replacing the Queen with a president chosen by Parliament. It was rejected by about 55 percent of voters and failed in every state.

claim: Gunmen assassinated French president Charles de Gaulle at Petit-Clamart in 1962.
record: OAS gunmen fired well over 100 rounds at de Gaulle's Citroën DS on 22 August 1962. Bullets passed inches from his head and two tyres were shot flat, but the driver sped away and no one in the car was hurt.

sources.title: 'Close shave!' How De Gaulle escaped assassin's bullets 60 years ago
sources.quote: Three of the bullets penetrate the bodywork and pass within inches of De Gaulle's head but he and his wife Yvonne miraculously escape unharmed.

claim: A Soviet submarine fired a nuclear torpedo at US warships during the Cuban Missile Crisis.
record: On 27 October 1962 US destroyers dropped signalling depth charges on submarine B-59. Crew accounts say the captain wanted to arm its nuclear torpedo; Vasili Arkhipov, whose agreement was reportedly needed, talked him down.

claim: In 1979 the US launched a nuclear counterstrike after NORAD's computers showed 1,400 Soviet missiles inbound.
record: A training tape loaded into NORAD's Cheyenne Mountain computers showed 1,400 Soviet ICBMs inbound. In the six minutes before satellite data proved it false, NORAD scrambled a dozen interceptors and launched the president's airborne command post; no missile was ever fired.

sources.title: False Warnings of Soviet Missile Attacks Put U.S. Forces on Alert in 1979-1980
sources.publisher: National Security Archive, George Washington University
sources.quote: warning displays showed... 1,400 Soviet ICBMs heading toward North America

claim: Captain FitzRoy refused to take Charles Darwin aboard the Beagle because of the shape of his nose.
record: Darwin later wrote that FitzRoy, a believer in physiognomy, doubted whether anyone with his nose could have enough energy for the voyage. FitzRoy took him anyway.

sources.title: The Autobiography of Charles Darwin
sources.quote: I had run a very narrow risk of being rejected, on account of the shape of my nose!

claim: Hubert Latham flew an aeroplane across the English Channel in July 1909.
record: Latham took off near Calais on 19 July 1909, but his engine failed eight miles out and he waited on his floating plane, smoking a cigarette. Blériot crossed on 25 July; two days later Latham ditched again, minutes short of Dover.

sources.title: British Civil Aviation in 1909
sources.quote: 19 July Englishman Hubert Latham attempts to fly the English Channel by aeroplane, but has to ditch his Antoinette IV due to engine trouble.

claim: Samuel Tilden, who won the popular vote in 1876, became president of the United States.
record: Tilden won the popular vote and led 184 to 165 in electoral votes, one short of a majority, with 20 votes from four states in dispute. A special commission split 8 to 7 along party lines and awarded all 20 to Rutherford B. Hayes.

sources.title: Disputed Election of 1876
sources.quote: The commission voted 8 to 7 to award the electoral votes from South Carolina, Florida, and Louisiana (and one from Oregon) to Hayes.

claim: The Great Seal of the United States depicts Moses parting the Red Sea.
record: In 1776 Benjamin Franklin proposed a Great Seal showing Moses drowning Pharaoh's army in the Red Sea. Congress tabled the design, and the seal finally adopted in 1782 showed a bald eagle instead.

sources.title: Great Seal of the United States

claim: Lincoln wrote the Gettysburg Address on the back of an envelope on the train.
record: Lincoln began drafting in Washington before he left and revised it in Gettysburg. The five known manuscript copies are on sheets of paper, not envelopes.

sources.title: Myths and mysteries about the Gettysburg Address
sources.quote: Lincoln started working on his remarks shortly after the battle was fought in July 1863, according to Lincoln experts

origin: The story appeared decades later and suited the image of Lincoln as an effortless genius.

claim: Thomas Edison personally electrocuted Topsy the elephant to show the dangers of his rival's AC power.
record: Topsy was killed at Coney Island's Luna Park in 1903 on the orders of the park's owners. There is no evidence Edison was involved, and the 'war of the currents' was long over.

sources.title: Topsy the Elephant Was a Victim of Her Captors, Not Thomas Edison
sources.quote: After all, the War of the Currents ended in the 1890s, while Topsy's death came later.

origin: The execution was filmed by the Edison Manufacturing Company, and its name on the film fused the two stories.

claim: The 1918 'Spanish flu' pandemic started in Spain.
record: Where the pandemic began is still debated, with theories pointing to the United States, France and China. Spain was neutral in World War I, and its uncensored press reported the outbreak openly, so the name stuck.

sources.title: The Spanish Influenza Pandemic: a lesson from history 100 years after 1918
sources.publisher: Journal of Preventive Medicine and Hygiene (via PubMed Central)
sources.quote: As Spain was neutral in the First World War, newspapers there were free to report the devastating effects that the 1918 pandemic virus was having in that country. Thus, it was generally perceived that the pandemic had originated in Spain, and the infection was incorrectly dubbed 'Spanish flu'.

origin: Wartime censors in the fighting nations suppressed flu news, so Spanish reports made it look like a Spanish disease.

claim: Cinco de Mayo celebrates Mexico's independence day.
record: Cinco de Mayo marks the Mexican army's victory over the French at the Battle of Puebla on 5 May 1862. Mexico's Independence Day is 16 September.
origin: The date became a big celebration of Mexican heritage in the United States, where many assume it marks independence.

claim: David Rice Atchison was president of the United States for one day in 1849.
record: Zachary Taylor's inauguration was delayed to Monday because 4 March fell on a Sunday. Taylor's term had legally begun anyway, and Atchison was never sworn in.

sources.title: No, David Rice Atchison Was Not 'President for a Day'
sources.quote: Atchison's existing term as senator and president pro tempore had ended at noon on March 4

origin: Atchison's supporters later promoted the claim, and his gravestone calls him 'President of the United States for one day'.

claim: Betsy Ross designed the first American flag at George Washington's request.
record: Betsy Ross was a real Philadelphia upholsterer who made flags, but no contemporary record shows she designed or made the first Stars and Stripes.

sources.title: Did Betsy Ross Really Make the First American Flag?
sources.quote: In fact, her story was first publicly relayed to the Historical Society of Pennsylvania nearly a century later, in 1870, by her grandson, William Canby.

origin: Her grandson William Canby told the story in a speech in 1870, nearly a century later, based on family tradition.

claim: The Liberty Bell cracked when it was rung to announce the Declaration of Independence.
record: No record shows the bell was rung for the Declaration in July 1776. The famous crack developed much later, most likely in the 1840s.

sources.title: The Liberty Bell
sources.publisher: National Park Service, Independence National Historical Park
sources.quote: While there is evidence that the bell rang to mark the Stamp Act tax and its repeal, there is no evidence that the bell rang on July 4 or 8, 1776.

origin: An 1847 short story by George Lippard invented the scene of an old bellman ringing the bell for independence.

claim: Workers who died building the Hoover Dam are buried inside its concrete.
record: The dam was poured in relatively shallow blocks, so a fallen worker would have been found quickly. The Bureau of Reclamation says no one is entombed in it.
origin: The dam's scale, and the roughly one hundred deaths during construction, made the grim rumour easy to believe.

claim: The ancient Maya predicted the world would end in 2012.
record: The Maya Long Count calendar completed a major cycle, a b'ak'tun, in December 2012, much like an odometer rolling over. Maya inscriptions mention dates far beyond 2012.
origin: New Age writers from the 1970s onward turned the calendar date into a prophecy of doom or transformation.

claim: Roman gladiators routinely greeted the emperor with 'We who are about to die salute you.'
record: The phrase is recorded for a single event, a staged naval battle on the Fucine Lake in 52 CE, described by Suetonius and Cassius Dio. Those fighters were condemned criminals and captives, and no source calls it a regular salute.

sources.title: Suetonius, The Life of Claudius, 21 (Loeb translation, J. C. Rolfe)
sources.quote: But when the combatants cried out: "Hail, emperor, they who are about to die salute thee," he replied, "Or not," and after that all of them refused to fight, maintaining that they had been pardoned.

origin: Nineteenth-century paintings, notably Jean-Léon Gérôme's, made it look like standard arena ritual.

claim: Columbus's crew feared they would sail off the edge of a flat Earth.
record: Educated Europeans had known the Earth was round since antiquity. The debate over Columbus was about its size: his critics correctly said Asia was much too far away.

sources.title: The Myth of the Flat Earth
sources.quote: It was he who invented the indelible picture of the young Columbus, a 'simple mariner,' appearing before a dark crowd of benighted inquisitors and hooded theologians at a council of Salamanca, all of whom believed, according to Irving, that the earth was flat like a plate.

origin: Washington Irving's romanticized 1828 biography of Columbus popularized the flat-Earth drama.

claim: Marie Antoinette responded to starving peasants with 'Let them eat cake.'
record: There is no evidence she said it. Jean-Jacques Rousseau attributed a similar line about brioche to 'a great princess' in his Confessions, written when Marie Antoinette was a child in Austria.
origin: Revolutionary pamphlets and later retellings pinned the arrogant remark on the unpopular queen.

claim: George Washington's false teeth were made of wood.
record: Washington's dentures were made from hippopotamus ivory, human teeth, animal teeth and metal springs. There is no evidence any were wooden.

sources.title: George Washington Didn't Have Wooden Teeth—They Were Ivory
sources.quote: Washington's dentures over the course of his lifetime used materials like human teeth along with bone and ivory from hippopotamus

origin: Stained, grainy ivory may have looked like wood, and the homespun image suited his legend.

claim: Galileo was thrown into a dungeon for saying the Earth goes around the Sun.
record: After his 1633 trial the Inquisition sentenced Galileo to imprisonment, but it was commuted to house arrest. He spent his last years at his villa in Arcetri and kept writing.

sources.title: 8 Things You May Not Know About Galileo
sources.quote: Although Galileo was given life behind bars, his sentence soon was changed to house arrest

origin: Retellings of the 'Eppur si muove' legend put him in a cell; a painting once attributed to Murillo shows him in a dungeon with the words on the wall.

claim: The US Senate ratified the Treaty of Versailles and took America into the League of Nations.
record: President Wilson championed the League, but the Senate rejected the treaty in November 1919 and again in March 1920, when it fell seven votes short of the two-thirds needed. The US never joined.

sources.title: The Paris Peace Conference and the Treaty of Versailles
sources.publisher: US Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.quote: In a final vote on March 19, 1920, the Treaty of Versailles fell short of ratification by seven votes.

claim: Allied troops invaded Japan's home islands in November 1945.
record: Operation Downfall planned landings on Kyushu for November 1945 and near Tokyo in 1946, the largest amphibious assault ever prepared. Japan announced its surrender in August, and the invasion was cancelled.

claim: Retreating German forces blew up Paris's bridges and landmarks in August 1944, as Hitler had ordered.
record: Hitler ordered that Paris should fall into Allied hands only as a field of ruins, and explosives were laid under bridges. The garrison commander, Dietrich von Choltitz, surrendered the city largely intact on 25 August.

claim: The United States bought Cuba from Spain in 1848.
record: President James K. Polk authorised an offer of $100 million for Cuba in 1848. Spain refused, and later American attempts to buy or seize the island also failed.

sources.title: An Abridged History of Cuban Independence
sources.quote: in 1848, US president James K. Polk formally offered the Spanish empire $100 million to purchase the island, an offer that Spain declined.

claim: Charles Babbage completed his Difference Engine for the British government in the 1830s.
record: The Treasury spent about £17,000, but work stopped in 1833 after a row with his engineer, leaving only a one-seventh demonstration section; the government formally gave up in 1842. The Science Museum finally built his later design, Difference Engine No. 2, in 1991, and it worked.

sources.title: Charles Babbage's Difference Engines and the Science Museum
sources.quote: was abruptly halted in 1833 following a dispute with Clement and the engine was never built.

claim: An Arab army captured Constantinople in 718.
record: The Umayyad Caliphate besieged the Byzantine capital by land and sea for about a year. Greek fire, a harsh winter, famine and Bulgarian attacks forced the survivors to retreat in 718.

claim: Napoleon's army crossed the English Channel and invaded Britain in 1805.
record: Napoleon massed around 200,000 men and a flotilla of invasion barges at Boulogne. Without control of the Channel he turned the army east against Austria in August 1805, and Trafalgar ended the threat that October.

sources.title: Napoleon%27s planned invasion of the United Kingdom

claim: Bonnie Prince Charlie's Jacobite army captured London in 1745.
record: The Jacobites reached Derby, about 125 miles from London, on 4 December 1745, causing panic in the capital. With no English rising or French landing in sight, their council voted on 5 December to turn back north.

sources.title: Jacobite Risings
sources.quote: On 4 December 1745, Charles entered Derby. He was now only 200km (125 miles) from London, but his army was tired and weakened by desertion.

claim: Britain went to war with the US in 1861 after Americans seized two Confederate envoys from a British ship.
record: A US warship stopped the British mail steamer Trent and removed Confederate diplomats. Britain sent thousands of troops to Canada and demanded an apology; Lincoln's government released the men, and war was avoided.

sources.title: The Trent Affair, 1861
sources.publisher: US Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.quote: The British, on the other hand, strongly protested Wilkes's action as illegal and a violation of their neutrality and demanded the release of the captive Confederate envoys as well as a formal apology.

claim: Samuel Langley's piloted Aerodrome flew over the Potomac in 1903, days before the Wright brothers.
record: Backed by War Department money, Langley's machine was catapulted from a houseboat twice in 1903. Both times it plunged into the Potomac; the second crash came on 8 December, nine days before the Wrights flew at Kitty Hawk.

claim: In 1958 Martin Luther King Jr. was stabbed in the chest at a Harlem book signing and survived.
record: Izola Ware Curry stabbed King with a letter opener that came to rest next to his aorta. Surgeons later told him that if he had sneezed he could have died.

sources.title: Izola Ware Curry
sources.publisher: The Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford University
sources.quote: Had Dr. King sneezed or coughed, the weapon would have penetrated the aorta.… He was just a sneeze away from death

claim: Emperor Nero played the fiddle while Rome burned in 64 CE.
record: The fiddle had not been invented. Tacitus says Nero was at Antium when the fire broke out, returned as it neared his palace and organised shelter and food; he reports the tale that Nero sang of Troy's fall only as a rumour.

sources.title: Tacitus, Annals, Book XV, 39 (Loeb translation, J. Jackson)
sources.quote: Nero, who at the time was staying in Antium, did not return to the capital until the fire was nearing the house by which he had connected the Palatine with the Gardens of Maecenas.

origin: Hostile ancient writers such as Suetonius and Cassius Dio reported the singing, and English retellings turned his lyre into a fiddle.

claim: The Pilgrims stepped ashore onto Plymouth Rock in 1620.
record: No account written by the Pilgrims mentions a rock. The boulder was pointed out in 1741, 121 years later, by Thomas Faunce, a church elder in his nineties, recalling what his father had told him as a boy.

sources.title: History of Plymouth Rock
sources.quote: Neither mentions a rock in their account of the landing.

origin: Thomas Faunce's 1741 identification turned an ordinary boulder into a national relic.

claim: Thomas Crapper invented the flush toilet.
record: Sir John Harington designed a flushing toilet in the 1590s, and Alexander Cumming patented the S-bend in 1775. Crapper was a Victorian plumber who ran a successful business and patented improvements such as the ballcock.
origin: A 1969 comic biography, 'Flushed with Pride', exaggerated his inventions, and his name on cisterns did the rest.

claim: The Great Chicago Fire of 1871 was started by Mrs O'Leary's cow kicking over a lantern.
record: The fire did start near the O'Leary barn, but no one proved how. In 1893 reporter Michael Ahern admitted he had invented the cow story, and the city council cleared Catherine O'Leary in 1997.

sources.title: Whodunit? The Mystery of Mrs. O'Leary's Cow
sources.quote: In 1997, they passed a resolution exonerating Catherine O'Leary and the cow. The City Council did not name an alternate culprit

origin: A reporter's colourful story played on prejudice against Irish immigrants and outlived every official finding.

claim: Albert Einstein worked at Los Alamos on the team that built the first atomic bomb.
record: Einstein signed the 1939 letter warning Roosevelt that Germany might build a bomb, but the Army judged him a security risk in 1940. He spent the war in Princeton, consulting for the US Navy on explosives, and never worked at Los Alamos.

sources.title: Albert Einstein
sources.publisher: Atomic Heritage Foundation (National Museum of Nuclear Science & History)
sources.quote: Einstein played no role in the Manhattan Project, having been denied a security clearance in July 1940 due to his pacifist tendencies.

origin: His famous equation and his signature on the letter tied his name to the bomb in public memory.

claim: The Titanic sent the first SOS distress call in history.
record: SOS was adopted as an international distress signal in 1906 and came into use from 1908, and ships used it before 1912. The Titanic's operators sent both the older CQD and SOS.

sources.title: Why Titanic's first call for help wasn't an SOS signal
sources.quote: An international group including the United Kingdom had ratified SOS as the official international distress signal four years earlier in 1908

origin: The disaster's fame made the Titanic's SOS the one everyone remembered.

claim: Napoleon's soldiers shot the nose off the Great Sphinx.
record: Drawings made decades before Napoleon's 1798 campaign already show the Sphinx without its nose. The 15th-century historian al-Maqrizi reported that a Sufi zealot damaged the face in 1378.
origin: Napoleon's famous Egyptian expedition made his troops convenient culprits.

claim: As a boy, George Washington chopped down his father's cherry tree and confessed: 'I cannot tell a lie.'
record: No evidence supports the tale. It first appeared in the fifth edition of Mason Locke Weems's biography of Washington, published in 1806, years after Washington's death.

sources.title: 5 Myths About George Washington, Debunked
sources.quote: the cherry tree story didn't appear until the fifth edition came out in 1806

origin: Parson Weems wrote moralizing, invented anecdotes to make Washington a model for children.

claim: Each Scottish clan has worn its own tartan pattern since ancient times.
record: Before the 18th century tartans varied by region and weaver rather than clan. Most 'clan tartans' were named and standardized in the 19th century, helped by the forged 1842 book 'Vestiarium Scoticum'.
origin: George IV's 1822 visit to Edinburgh set off a Highland craze, and manufacturers happily assigned patterns to clans.

claim: Saint Patrick drove the snakes out of Ireland.
record: Ireland's fossil record shows no sign of native snakes at all. The island was too cold for reptiles during the last Ice Age, and rising seas cut it off from Britain before snakes could arrive.

sources.title: Did St. Patrick Really Drive Snakes Out of Ireland?
sources.quote: At no time has there ever been any suggestion of snakes in Ireland.

origin: The story, first recorded centuries after Patrick's death, is usually read as a metaphor for his driving out paganism.

claim: Friday the 13th became unlucky because the Knights Templar were arrested on that day in 1307.
record: The Templars were arrested in France on Friday, 13 October 1307, but no record links the date to bad luck until the 20th century. Fear of Friday the 13th as such appears in writing only from the 19th century.
origin: Novels, most famously 'The Da Vinci Code', popularized the Templar connection.
